events.text: Under the old pine at the crossroads somebody has scratched a xiangqi board into a flat stone. Every evening {npc}, who mends nets for a living, sits there alone with a bag of wooden pieces and waits for an opponent. Tonight {he} looks up at you and rattles the bag.

choices.text: Sit down and play

mem.note: sat down at the pine board

effects.log: You lose in thirty moves. {npc} sets the pieces up again without a word. You lose in forty. It is dark when you walk home, and you are already planning tomorrow.

choices.text: Watch a game first

effects.log: You watch {npc} beat a passing pedlar, a monk and a boy of twelve. Then {he} points at the empty seat. You know {his} openings now, and you still lose.

events.text: Five years of evenings. You and {npc} keep the score in chalk on the trunk of the pine: tally marks, hundreds of them, and yours are fewer. Tonight, for the first time, you see a win six moves ahead.

choices.text: Take the win

effects.log: Checkmate. {npc} stares at the board for a long time, then laughs so hard the crows leave the pine. {He} carves your mark into the bark with a knife instead of chalk.

choices.text: Let the win go by, and see what {he} does

mem.note: let a win go by for the game

effects.log: You play the quiet move. {npc} looks at you sharply. 'You saw it.' 'Saw what?' The next evening {he} brings a jug of wine and the best game of your life.

events.text: The tally marks on the pine have climbed above your heads and around the trunk twice. {npc}'s eyes are going: {he} holds each piece close to read it, and twice tonight {he} has moved your horse thinking it was {his} own.

choices.text: Say nothing and play on

mem.note: let me win the blind game

effects.log: You let the wrong horse stand and lose by it. {npc} wins, and is so pleased that you would lose a hundred games for that face.

choices.text: Carve the pieces deep so they can be read by touch

mem.note: carved me pieces I could feel

effects.log: It takes you a month with a small knife. {npc} runs a thumb over the general and smiles. {He} plays by feel from then on, and plays better.

choices.text: Call out every move aloud

effects.log: You become the board's voice: 'Cannon to the fifth file.' Passers-by stop to listen, and soon the whole crossroads is arguing about your games.

events.text: {npc} does not come to the pine this evening, or the next. On the third day a grandchild of {his} brings you the bag of pieces. {npc} died in sleep, the child says, and wanted you to have them.

choices.text: Play one last game against the empty seat

effects.log: You play both sides until the stars are out. Black wins; it was always going to. You add one tally mark for {npc} on the pine, at the very top.

choices.text: Teach the grandchild the opening {npc} always used

effects.log: The child is slow, then suddenly not. Next spring there is a new name chalked on the pine, under yours.

choices.text: Leave the pieces on the stone for whoever comes

effects.log: In the morning they are set up for a game. Nobody admits to it. The board under the pine is never empty again.

events.text: At an inn on the road you share a table with {npc}, a traveller going home to the far side of the empire. You talk until the lamp gutters. In the morning {he} writes an address on a scrap of paper. 'Write. The caravans are slow, but they get there.'

choices.text: Write the first letter that same week

effects.log: You write four pages about nothing: the weather, the price of rice, a dog that steals shoes. Eight months later an answer comes, six pages, about a goat.

choices.text: Keep the scrap and mean to write

mem.note: had to be written to first

effects.log: You mean to. The scrap lives in your sleeve, then a drawer. A letter comes from {npc} anyway, the next spring: 'I suppose you lost my address. Here it is again.'

events.text: Letters every year now, crossing on the road. You have never seen {npc} again, but you know the name of {his} every hen. This letter says {his} house burned down in the dry season. Everyone lived. Everything else is ash.

choices.text: Send money with the next caravan (20 taels)

mem.note: sent silver when the house burned

effects.log: The caravan master counts it twice in front of you. {npc}'s answer is one line long and smudged: 'I did not know anyone so far away could reach this far.'

choices.text: Send a long letter and a packet of seeds from your garden

mem.note: sent seeds for the new garden

effects.log: Next year a letter comes with a pressed flower in it: your gourds grew up the new wall of the new house.

events.text: Thirty years of letters fill a chest. One morning there is a knock instead of a letter: {npc}, grey and stooped and grinning, with a walking staff and a goat on a rope. 'I wanted to see if you are as tall as you write.'

choices.text: Take {him} round every place you ever wrote about

mem.note: showed me the town I knew by letter

effects.log: The shoe-stealing dog's grandson, the wineshop, the crooked bridge. {npc} knows them all already and is delighted that they are real.

choices.text: Sit up all night reading the old letters together

mem.note: read our letters aloud with me

effects.log: You read each other's handwriting out loud and argue about what you meant. By dawn you have laughed yourselves hoarse.

events.text: A letter comes in an unfamiliar hand. {npc}'s child writes that {npc} is very ill, and asks for you by name, and keeps your last letter unopened beside the bed, saving it for a good day. By the time you read this, the child writes, it may be over.

choices.text: Write back to the child

effects.log: You write the way you always wrote: the weather, the rice, a dog. A year later the child writes again. {npc} went quietly, with your letter read at last. The caravans keep running.

choices.text: Burn one letter at the crossroads, to send it on

effects.log: It goes up in a single bright sheet. You stand there until the smoke has gone east, the way the caravans go. Later word comes that {npc} died that same evening.

events.arc: The Worst Fisher on the River
events.text: {npc} has fished the same bend of the river for six years and never caught anything. Everyone knows it. You sit down on the bank one evening because there is no other shade, and {npc} offers you a second rod.

choices.text: Take the rod

effects.log: Neither of you catches anything. {npc} explains, at length, the habits of fish {he} has never seen. It is the most restful evening you have had in a year.

choices.text: Show {him} how you were taught to bait a hook

mem.note: tried to teach me to fish

effects.log: {npc} watches carefully, nods, and does it wrong. 'I prefer my way,' {he} says. 'It is more peaceful for the fish.'

events.arc: The Worst Fisher on the River
events.text: Years of evenings on the bank. Tonight the line in {npc}'s hands goes tight enough to sing. Something huge is on it, and {npc} has no idea what to do.

choices.text: Wade in and help land it

mem.note: helped me land the great carp

ok.log: A carp as long as your arm, gold at the gills. {npc} holds it up for the whole river to see, then, shaking, lets it go. 'Now they know I could,' {he} says.

mem.note: fell in the river with me

fail.log: You both go into the river. The fish goes the other way. {npc} sits in the shallows, soaked, laughing too hard to stand.

choices.text: Shout advice from the bank

effects.log: Your advice is contradictory and loud. The fish takes the hook and the rod and leaves. {npc} says it was the best moment of {his} life.

events.arc: The Worst Fisher on the River
events.text: {npc} is too old to walk to the bend now. You find {him} in a chair by the window, looking toward the river.

choices.text: Carry {him} down to the bank once more

mem.note: carried me down to the river

effects.log: It takes you an hour and every bit of your breath. {npc} holds the rod the whole afternoon and catches nothing, which is exactly right.

choices.text: Bring the river to {him}: a bucket with a minnow in it

mem.note: brought me a minnow in a bucket

effects.log: {npc} watches the minnow go round for hours. 'Finally,' {he} says. 'One that cannot get away.'

choices.text: Tell {him} the story of the great carp, bigger every time

effects.log: By the end of the visit the carp was as long as a boat and pulled you both to the sea. {npc} corrects you: 'Two boats.'

events.text: Outside the wineshop there is a bench that fits three. On it most evenings: {npc}, a cooper who thinks every barrel has a temper, and an old tea porter with one boot. The cooper shifts up and pats the wood.

choices.text: Sit and have one cup of tea

mem.note: took the third seat on the bench

effects.log: The cooper explains the moods of barrels. The porter tells you about the boot. By the third evening you have opinions about both.

choices.text: Buy the round (3 taels)

effects.log: Three cups of the cheap yellow wine for them and a pot of tea for you, and you are a regular. The wineshop keeper writes your name on the wall beside theirs.

events.text: The tea porter does not come one evening. The bench is wrong with two. {npc} turns {his} cup round and round.

choices.text: Go and find out

mem.note: carried wine up the hill road with me

effects.log: The porter has fallen on the hill road and broken an ankle. You and {npc} carry wine up to the hut for six weeks, and the bench moves indoors, round a bed.

choices.text: Keep the seat for the porter

effects.log: You put the boot on the empty end of the bench, the one boot. The porter comes back in the spring, limping, and laughs at it for a full minute.

events.text: {npc} tells you the cooperage is moving downriver, where the timber is. {He} will go with it. The bench will be two again.

choices.text: Carve all three names on the bench before {he} goes

mem.note: carved my name on the bench

effects.log: You do it badly with a kitchen knife. The keeper threatens to charge you for the bench, then varnishes it instead.

choices.text: Promise to visit downriver every autumn

effects.log: You keep it for nine years. The new town has a bench too. It fits three.

choices.text: Tell {him} to go, and be glad

effects.log: {npc} looks at you a long moment. 'I thought you would be sad.' 'I am. Go anyway.' {He} goes, and writes, and the wine at the bench tastes thinner for a year.

events.text: The wall between your yard and {npc}'s has fallen in the rains. When you go to rebuild it, {npc} is already there with a string line, and the string is a hand's width into your yard.

choices.text: Argue the hand's width

mem.note: fought me for a hand of mud

effects.log: You argue it for a week. The whole lane takes sides. The wall goes up exactly on the old line, and you and {npc} stop speaking.

choices.text: Let {him} have it

mem.note: let me have the hand of ground

effects.log: {npc} looks suspicious, then embarrassed, then plants a row of beans in the hand's width and brings you the first basket. Some things grow better than arguments.

events.text: Ten years of a wall between you. {npc} has nodded to you four times, all at funerals. Tonight there is a shout from over the wall: {npc}'s roof beam has cracked, and the snow is coming.

choices.text: Climb the wall with a lantern and a prop

mem.note: held up my roof in the snow

effects.log: You hold the beam with your shoulder while {npc} wedges the prop. When it holds, you are both white with plaster. 'Hand's width,' {npc} says. 'Yours.'

choices.text: Send the lad from the corner over with rope

effects.log: The roof holds. In the morning there is a jar of pickled radish on the wall, with no note. You eat it all winter.

events.text: {npc} knocks at your gate with a mallet in one hand. 'That wall,' {npc} says, 'has always been ugly.'

choices.text: Knock a gate through it together

mem.note: knocked a gate through our wall

effects.log: It takes a day. The little gate is crooked, and neither of you will ever fix it. Children will run through it for fifty years.

choices.text: Plant a gourd vine on it instead, to share

effects.log: The gourds hang on both sides. You argue every autumn about which ones are whose, and both of you enjoy it.

events.text: The bean row in the hand's width has fed both houses for years. {npc} is at your gate with a mallet. 'That wall,' {npc} says, 'is in the way of my beans.'

choices.text: Knock it down, and share the yard

mem.note: took down the wall with me

effects.log: One yard, two houses, a great many beans. The lane calls it the Bean Treaty and other neighbours start to argue less.

choices.text: Keep the wall but cut a window in it

mem.note: cut a window in the wall

effects.log: Through the little window you pass tea, gossip and, once, a cat. It is the best window in the province.

events.text: {npc} sells noodles from a stall at the bridge foot, and the broth is so good that people from three streets away queue in the rain. {npc} will not say what is in it, not for silver, not for wine.

choices.text: Eat there every day until you can guess

mem.note: ate at my stall every day

effects.log: In a year you have guessed star anise, dried shrimp and patience. {npc} laughs. 'Three out of eleven.'

choices.text: Help carry the pots up from the river each dawn

effects.log: The pots are heavy and {npc} is getting old. In return you eat for nothing and are told nothing.

events.text: {npc}'s hands have begun to shake too much to pull noodles. No child of {his} wants the stall. One night {npc} sits you down at the back. 'The broth,' {he} says. 'Do you want it?'

choices.text: Learn it, all eleven

effects.log: It takes a winter. The eleventh is a slice of dried tangerine peel older than you are. You promise never to tell.

choices.text: Find a young cook who needs a trade

mem.note: found the stall a new cook

effects.log: A sharp-eyed orphan from the docks learns it in your place. {npc} grumbles for a month and then says the child's broth is better than {his} own.

events.text: The stall at the bridge foot still queues in the rain. A food writer from the capital has called the broth the best in the province, and is asking around for the secret.

choices.text: Keep the secret

effects.log: The writer offers 50 taels for it and you say no. The writer calls the stall overrated. The queue gets longer.

choices.text: Tell the writer: 'patience'

effects.log: It is written down with great care. The writer goes away delighted with a word. Nobody can make the broth from a word.

choices.text: Cook a bowl yourself and let the writer guess

effects.log: Three out of eleven. You smile exactly the way {npc} used to.

events.text: You and {npc} have known each other since your knees worked. Tonight, over a third cup, {npc} says: 'We never swore to be siblings. Everyone in the stories swears. We should do it before one of us forgets how.'

choices.text: Do it now, in the peach orchard

mem.note: swore to me among bare peach trees

effects.log: There are no peaches, it is winter, and you both have to be helped up off your knees afterward. It is the best oath ever sworn.

choices.text: Do it properly: incense, witnesses, a feast (10 taels)

mem.note: swore to me before the whole lane

effects.log: Half the lane comes. Someone's child writes the oath in crooked characters. You both cry and blame the incense.

choices.text: Laugh: 'We are already worse than sworn'

effects.log: {npc} laughs too, and nods, and does not mention it again. But you notice that you are called 'elder sibling' from then on.

events.text: The oath has given you both ideas. {npc} wants to go and see the place where, in the stories, the three heroes swore. It is four days' walk, and neither of you has walked four days in ten years.

choices.text: Go, slowly

mem.note: walked nine days to a tea stall with me

effects.log: It takes nine days. The famous spot is a yard for ox-carts and a tea stall. You drink the tea and agree it was worth it.

choices.text: Hire a cart (5 taels)

mem.note: rode the cart and argued the story with me

effects.log: The carter tells you the whole story wrong. You both correct the carter all the way there and back.

events.text: {npc} is dying, and knows it, and is cheerful about it. 'The oath said same day,' {npc} says. 'Do not you dare.'

choices.text: Promise to live another twenty years out of spite

effects.log: {npc} laughs until {he} coughs. 'Good. Tell me about them.' {He} dies that night, still smiling at the joke.

choices.text: Sit with {him} and recite the oath one more time

effects.log: You get through it together, both voices thin. At the line about the same day, {npc} squeezes your hand: no.

events.text: {npc}'s hens have discovered your vegetable patch. There are seven of them. The cabbages are now lace.

choices.text: Complain over the wall

effects.log: {npc} is mortified and pays you in eggs: one a day until the cabbages grow back. You end up with more eggs than cabbages ever gave you.

choices.text: Build a fence of woven willow

mem.note: made me laugh with the fence

effects.log: It takes three days and the hens are over it in three minutes. {npc} comes to watch and laughs until {he} has to sit down.

events.text: The egg treaty has held for years. Now it has a problem: one of the hens has hatched a rooster, and the rooster crows at the fourth watch, under your window.

choices.text: Negotiate: the rooster for a jar of your plum wine

effects.log: {npc} accepts too quickly. The rooster goes to a cousin in the next village. Peace returns, and {npc} drinks the wine and admits to hating the rooster too.

choices.text: Learn to sleep through it

effects.log: It takes a month. Afterwards you sleep so well that you are late for everything for the rest of your life.

events.text: {npc}'s last old hen, the cabbage-eater, the founder of the treaty, has died. {npc} is surprisingly sad about it.

choices.text: Help bury the hen under your cabbages

mem.note: buried the old hen with me

effects.log: You plant a cabbage on top. It grows enormous. Neither of you can bring yourselves to eat it.

choices.text: Bring {him} a chick from the market (1 tael)

effects.log: {npc} names it after you. It grows up and eats your cabbages. The treaty is renewed.

events.text: A new neighbour, {npc}, practises the suona every morning at first light. The suona is a horn built for weddings and funerals in the open air. It is not built for a lane this narrow.

choices.text: Knock and ask for a later hour

effects.log: {npc} apologises and moves practice to noon, when the lane is at market, and plays you a tune by way of sorry. It is actually lovely, at noon.

choices.text: Put cotton in your ears and endure

effects.log: A month of cotton. Then one morning you notice that you are humming the tune while you wash.

events.text: A family down the lane has lost their grandmother, and cannot afford funeral musicians. {npc} is standing in the lane with the suona under one arm, looking unsure.

choices.text: Tell {him}: play, and you will beat the drum

effects.log: You have never beaten a funeral drum in your life. Nobody notices. {npc}'s horn carries the old woman all the way up the hill.

choices.text: Lend {him} your good mourning clothes

effects.log: {npc} plays in borrowed white. Afterwards {npc} is hired for every funeral in the district.

events.text: {npc} comes to you with the suona wrapped in red cloth. 'I want to make an arrangement. When it is your time, I play. When it is mine, you find someone good. Not the one from the next village. Flat.'

choices.text: Agree, and shake on it

mem.note: made the funeral pact with me

effects.log: You shake on it. Then {npc} plays your funeral tune for you, now, so that you can hear it. It is wonderful. You ask for it twice.

choices.text: Ask {him} to teach you to play instead

effects.log: Your first note sounds like a goose that has been sat on. The whole lane comes out. {npc} cannot stop laughing long enough to teach you anything for a week.

events.text: Old Auntie Gu at the corner well knows everything: who owes whom, whose son failed the county exam, which rooster has been dreaming. Every morning she watches you draw water and comments.

choices.text: Talk back

effects.log: 'Your bucket is too small.' 'Your opinions are too big.' Auntie Gu cackles. From then on she saves you the cold water from the bottom of the well on hot days.

choices.text: Ask her what she knows about the house you live in

effects.log: She knows too much: the builder lost it in a quarrel over a goat. She tells you where the loose brick with the old coins is.

events.text: Auntie Gu has not been at the well for three mornings. Her door is shut, and the lane has noticed, and nobody has knocked.

choices.text: Knock

effects.log: She has a fever and has been too proud to call. You bring broth for a week. She criticises the salt in every bowl and eats them all.

choices.text: Tell the lane, and set up a rota

effects.log: Six households, one bowl each a day. Auntie Gu is outraged to be helped, and recovers, and knows even more about everyone afterward.

events.text: Auntie Gu has died at ninety-one, at the well, in the middle of a sentence about the tax collector's nephew. Her niece brings you a small box. Inside is a ledger of the whole lane for sixty years.

choices.text: Read it, all of it

effects.log: It is full of secrets, and all of them are kind: who paid whose debt in the dark, who left rice on whose step. You never look at the lane the same way.

choices.text: Burn it unread at her grave

effects.log: The smoke goes straight up. You keep only one page, the one with your own name on it. It says: 'good bucket arm.'

events.text: The persimmon tree in {npc}'s yard leans over your wall, and every autumn half its fruit hangs on your side, orange as lanterns. The old custom is unclear.

choices.text: Pick only what falls

effects.log: You eat the windfalls and leave the rest. {npc} sees this and, the next day, hands a whole basket over the wall. 'You are too polite. It makes the tree nervous.'

choices.text: Ask {him} over to pick them together

effects.log: You do it from both sides of the wall with long poles, and the tree is stripped in an hour. You dry them on strings under both your eaves.

events.text: A storm has cracked the persimmon's great branch, the one over your wall. A carpenter says it must come off, or the tree will split.

choices.text: Prop it with a forked pole instead

effects.log: The carpenter says it will not work. It works for twenty years. The prop becomes a part of the tree.

choices.text: Let it be cut, and carve the wood into something

effects.log: You carve two spoons from the branch, one for each house. {npc} uses {his} every day.

events.text: The persimmon is old now, and so are you both. This autumn the crows have taken most of it, and there are just three fruit left at the top, glowing in the cold.

choices.text: Leave them for the crows, as the old custom says

effects.log: {npc} nods. 'Something should have something.' You sit on either side of the wall and watch the crows argue.

choices.text: Climb for them

ok.log: Three persimmons, and you down the tree with all your bones. You eat one each, and the third goes on the little shrine in {npc}'s yard.

fail.log: You get one, and then the ladder decides otherwise. A bruised hip and a split persimmon. {npc} eats the split one and pronounces it the best.

events.text: {npc} next door has failed the provincial examination four times. Every three years {npc} packs a box of brushes and a cold rice cake and walks to the provincial capital. This is the fifth time.

choices.text: Give {him} a better rice cake for the road

mem.note: gave me a rice cake for the road

effects.log: {npc} fails again, but writes that the rice cake was the best part of the trip. 'Next time.'

choices.text: Help {him} study: you read the classics aloud while {he} writes

effects.log: You learn the Analects backward. {npc} fails by two places, the closest yet.

events.text: {npc} is going for the ninth time. {His} hair is grey, and the other candidates are young enough to be {his} children. Some of them laugh.

choices.text: Walk {him} to the edge of town and say the right thing

mem.note: said the right thing at the town edge

effects.log: 'You are not going because you will pass. You are going because you are the kind of person who goes.' {npc} stands a little straighter.

choices.text: Ask {him} gently if it is time to stop

effects.log: {npc} thinks for a long time. 'One more,' {he} says. 'Then I will teach children who will pass.'

events.text: News from the provincial capital: {npc} has passed, on the eleventh attempt, the oldest graduate in living memory. The whole lane is drunk by noon.

choices.text: Hang the red banner yourself

effects.log: You climb the gate with a banner bigger than you. {npc} cries in the lane and everyone pretends it is the firecracker smoke.

choices.text: Give {him} the brush you bought for this day years ago

mem.note: kept a brush for my day

effects.log: {npc} weighs it in {his} hand. 'You believed it before I did.' {He} writes your name with it first.

events.text: A family from the northern frontier has taken the empty house at the end of the lane. They speak with flat vowels, eat noodles at breakfast, and the lane does not know what to make of them. {npc}, the eldest, stands at the gate looking lost.

choices.text: Bring a basket of local greens and say welcome

effects.log: {npc} sends the basket back full of dumplings the size of your fist. The lane, sniffing the air, comes round within a week.

choices.text: Ask {him} to teach you to fold northern dumplings

effects.log: Your dumplings come apart in the pot. {npc} laughs, the first laugh in that house since the move, and shows you again.

events.text: Winter. The northerners are the only people in the lane who are not cold. {npc} cannot understand why your houses have no heated brick beds.

choices.text: Let {him} build one in your house (8 taels)

effects.log: A kang, a heated brick bed, the first in the district. You sleep warm for the first winter of your life and the whole lane queues to sit on it.

choices.text: Teach {him} the local way: more quilts and complaining

mem.note: complained about the cold with me

effects.log: {npc} tries it for a week and declares it barbaric. You become friends through the complaining.

events.text: {npc}'s youngest is marrying a local from the next lane. Two kinds of wedding food, two kinds of song, and two grandmothers with opinions. {npc} asks you to stand between the families as go-between.

choices.text: Do it, and make both grandmothers laugh

effects.log: You tell each grandmother privately that the other grandmother is jealous of those dumplings. By the wedding they are swapping recipes and plotting the next one.

choices.text: Keep it simple: one table of each food

effects.log: The guests eat both and argue about which is better until the moon is up. Everyone agrees it was the best wedding in years.

events.text: Before New Year every door needs a pair of red couplets, and the calligrapher who wrote them for the lane has died. The neighbours look at you, because you once wrote a letter for someone.

choices.text: Write them all

effects.log: Forty doors. Your hand cramps and your characters wander. But on New Year's morning the whole lane is red with your writing.

choices.text: Write only your own, and well

effects.log: One perfect pair. The neighbours come to look and go away and copy it, badly, so the whole lane says the same thing in forty hands.

events.text: Every New Year now, the lane brings you red paper. This year a widow asks for something that is not a proverb: her late husband's favourite line, from a song he always sang badly.

choices.text: Write the song line as it is

effects.log: It does not scan and it does not rhyme. She weeps at her door, and every passer-by stops to read it.

choices.text: Make the line into a proper couplet

effects.log: You turn the bad song into a good couplet. She reads it and laughs: 'He never sang it so well.'

events.text: Your hand is not steady enough for big characters any more. On the morning of New Year's Eve a neighbour's child is at your door, holding the red paper and a brush. 'Show me.'

choices.text: Guide the child's hand on the first pair

effects.log: Your hand over the small one. The strokes come out half yours, half the child's. The door wears them proudly.

choices.text: Let the child write and only correct the last stroke

effects.log: Wobbly, brave characters. Next year the child writes the whole lane, and saves the last stroke of each for you.

events.text: On the night of the Lantern Festival the riddles hang from every lantern in the market street, and whoever guesses one tears it off and wins a sweet. One lantern at the end, a plain white one, has a riddle nobody has guessed in three years. It is signed only with a little drawing of a crane.

choices.text: Puzzle it out

ok.log: 'A mouth on top of a mouth, a roof with no house.' It is a character, folded twice. You tear the paper off and the crowd cheers. On the back, in tiny writing: 'Next year.'

fail.log: You stand under it until the lanterns are put out and you still do not have it. Walking home, you laugh, and the answer is still not there.

choices.text: Buy a sweet and watch others try

effects.log: A scholar, a fishwife and a child all fail at the crane lantern. The fishwife swears at it with real art. It is the best show at the festival.

events.text: Every Lantern Festival since, the crane lantern has had a new riddle, and it is always harder. This year you see who hangs it: {npc}, an old lantern-maker with paper cuts on every finger, who looks at you and smiles as if you were a puzzle too.

choices.text: Ask {him} for the answer to the first one

effects.log: 'Ah,' {npc} says. 'That was the year I found out who in this town likes to think.' {He} gives you a crane lantern of your own.

choices.text: Tell {him} the answers you got right, and the ones you did not

mem.note: told me the wrong answers too

effects.log: {npc} listens to every wrong answer with real pleasure. 'Those are better than mine,' {he} says, and writes one down.

choices.text: Hang a riddle of your own beside {his}

effects.log: Your riddle is guessed in four minutes by a seven-year-old. {npc} laughs until {his} lantern swings.

events.text: {npc} is too old now to climb the ladder with the crane lantern. {He} gives it to you, folded flat, with a box of riddles written in a careful hand. 'One a year,' {he} says. 'There are forty. Do not rush.'

choices.text: Hang it, and never tell anyone who writes them

effects.log: For years the town argues about who the Riddler is. You join in the arguing and guess wrong on purpose.

choices.text: Hang it, and write a new riddle of your own each year after the forty

effects.log: Your riddles are worse and the town loves them more. On the forty-first year, {npc}'s handwriting is gone and yours is the crane's.

events.text: The village dragon boat lost its fourth oar to a sprained shoulder a week before the Dragon Boat Festival. The drummer, {npc}, is going door to door. 'You have arms,' {npc} says at yours. 'That is the whole qualification.'

choices.text: Join the crew

effects.log: Twelve days of dawn practice on the river. Your palms blister, then harden. You learn to pull on the drum and not on your own idea of when.

choices.text: Offer to make the rice dumplings for the crew instead

effects.log: Two hundred zongzi in bamboo leaves. The crew eats them all in a single afternoon and says you are the real fourth oar.

events.text: Race day. The river is lined with people and the drums of nine villages. Your boat is the oldest and its dragon head has lost an eye. {npc} raises the drumstick.

choices.text: Pull with everything you have

ok.log: Third of nine. Nobody expected you to finish. The village carries the crew home on its shoulders and someone paints a new eye on the dragon.

mem.note: went into the bank with us

fail.log: You catch a crab with the oar and the boat slews into the bank. Last, wet and laughing. The village carries you home anyway.

choices.text: Keep the rhythm and save the crew's strength for the last stretch

effects.log: You hold the stroke while the others burn out. Over the last hundred lengths your boat passes four others. Fifth, and the proudest fifth in the river's history.

events.text: Every year since you have pulled the fourth oar. Now {npc} has grown too old to drum, and the crew wants you to take the drum.

choices.text: Take the drum

effects.log: From the drum you can see every face in the boat. You beat the old rhythm, and the young crew pulls a little too fast, the way you once did.

choices.text: Keep your oar and find a young drummer

effects.log: A loud child with no sense of rhythm, who learns one. {npc} sits on the bank and shouts corrections at the drum all race long.

events.text: At the Mid-Autumn Festival you bake mooncakes for the first time, in a borrowed mould, and one of them comes out with the pattern upside down and the stamp of the old bakery that used to stand in your lane: a rabbit and a single character, 'return'.

choices.text: Ask around about the old bakery

effects.log: An old porter remembers it: the baker hid letters in mooncakes for lovers who could not meet. The mould you borrowed was the baker's own.

choices.text: Eat it under the moon and think no more about it

effects.log: It is a little burnt and very good. You sit in the yard until the moon is small.

events.text: Next Mid-Autumn the mould's owner, an old widow, comes asking for it back. When you give it to her, she turns it in her hands. 'This was my mother's,' she says. 'She baked the letters.'

choices.text: Ask her to bake with you

effects.log: She shows you how to fold a paper slip into the paste so it does not burn. You bake a tray together, each with a slip that says something kind.

choices.text: Give her the burnt one you saved

effects.log: She laughs at it and cries a little. 'Return,' she reads. 'She always said everything does.'

events.text: Every Mid-Autumn now there is a tray of mooncakes with slips folded inside, handed out at your gate. This year a stranger comes back to it: years ago a slip said 'go home', and the stranger did, and made peace with a brother.

choices.text: Bake one with the stranger's brother's name in it

effects.log: The stranger takes it home wrapped in red cloth. Next year two people come to your gate.

choices.text: Ask the stranger to write the next year's slips

effects.log: The stranger's slips are better than yours: short, odd, true. 'Your dog misses you.' 'Eat the orange.'

events.text: At Qingming, sweeping the family graves on the hillside, you notice a grave beside the path that nobody sweeps. The stone has sunk sideways. The name on it is nearly gone.

choices.text: Sweep it too

effects.log: It takes a little longer. You pull the weeds, right the stone with your shoulder and leave one stick of incense. On the way down you feel lighter, for no good reason.

choices.text: Try to read the name

effects.log: Rubbing it with charcoal, you make out a surname and the words 'ferry keeper'. Nobody in the village knows it.

events.text: You have swept the ferry keeper's grave every Qingming since. This year someone has been there before you: fresh incense, and a bowl of rice with a pair of chopsticks laid across it.

choices.text: Wait on the path to see who comes

effects.log: At dusk an old boatman climbs up with a second bowl. 'My grandfather,' the boatman says. 'I thought nobody else remembered him. Then the grave started being swept.'

choices.text: Leave a note under the stone

effects.log: Next year there is a note back: 'Thank you. He ferried people for free in the flood year. Nobody wrote it down.'

events.text: The old boatman's family now sweep the ferry keeper's grave. This Qingming, when you reach it, there is a new stone beside it, smaller, with your name and the words: 'who swept it when nobody did'. It is blank where the date of death goes. 'For later,' the boatman says. 'No hurry.'

choices.text: Laugh and thank them

effects.log: You laugh so hard you have to sit on your own gravestone. The boatman's grandchildren think it is the funniest thing they have ever seen.

choices.text: Ask that it say 'ferry passenger' instead

effects.log: They change it. You like it better: one more person the ferry keeper carried across.

events.arc: Up the Hill at Double Ninth
events.text: On the ninth day of the ninth month people climb high places, drink chrysanthemum wine and wear a sprig of dogwood against bad luck. {npc} and a few friends from the lane ask you to make up their number for the hill.

choices.text: Go, and carry the wine

effects.log: Six of you on the hill, the whole valley gold below. Someone makes a bad poem, someone makes a worse one, and you laugh until the sun goes.

choices.text: Go, and bring cakes for the wind

effects.log: You cut the double-ninth cake on the summit stone. The wind takes your dogwood sprig and {npc} declares that your bad luck has blown to the next province.

events.arc: Up the Hill at Double Ninth
events.text: The Double Ninth again. There are four of you on the hill this year. One has moved to the coast and one has died. {npc} pours an extra cup and sets it on the stone.

choices.text: Make the bad poem the missing friend used to make

mem.note: made the bad poem for the one who is gone

effects.log: You make it worse on purpose. {npc} laughs and then has to look at the valley for a while.

choices.text: Pour the extra cup out over the hill

effects.log: The wine soaks into the thin soil. 'Next year,' {npc} says, 'we will pour two.'

events.arc: Up the Hill at Double Ninth
events.text: Double Ninth. It is only you and {npc} now, and the hill has become very steep. You stop four times on the path. At the top, {npc} sits down on the summit stone and says, 'I think this is my last climb.'

choices.text: 'Then we will carry you up next year'

effects.log: {npc} laughs. 'You will not.' You do, the next year, with two young neighbours and a chair on poles. {npc} complains the whole way up and weeps at the top.

choices.text: Sit beside {him} until the sun goes

mem.note: watched the last sunset on the hill with me

effects.log: Neither of you says anything. The valley goes gold, then blue. You put your dogwood sprig in {npc}'s collar, for luck, and walk down very slowly together.

events.text: The first snow of the year comes in the night. In the morning your spouse is up before you, sweeping a circle in the yard and setting out two stools and a teapot in the middle of it.

choices.text: Go out in your quilt

effects.log: You drink tea in the snow, wrapped in quilts, and watch the snow fill the circle in. Neither of you is cold. It becomes a thing you do.

choices.text: Bring out the good tea you were saving

effects.log: The good tea in the first snow. Your spouse looks at the tin and then at you. 'What were you saving it for?' 'This, apparently.'

events.text: The first snow again, and the stools, and the teapot. Your spouse has been ill this winter and is thin in the quilt. 'We are not missing it,' your spouse says.

choices.text: Carry the stools closer to the door

effects.log: Your circle is small this year, right against the step. It is still a circle. Your spouse recovers by spring, and says it was the tea.

choices.text: Make the tea inside, at the open window

effects.log: The snow comes in at the window and melts on the table. It counts. You both decide it counts.

events.text: You are both old. The first snow comes, and you find your spouse already sweeping the circle, slowly, with a broom taller than either of you remembers it being.

choices.text: Take the other end of the broom

effects.log: Two people sweeping one circle very badly. The tea goes cold. You make more.

choices.text: Tell your spouse the first time again, as a story

effects.log: You tell it wrong on purpose and get corrected. By the end you have both remembered things neither of you knew you had kept.

events.arc: A Walk-On at the Temple Fair
events.text: A travelling opera troupe has come for the temple fair, and their soldier with no lines has run off with a fishmonger. The troupe master, {npc}, looks at you in the crowd. 'You. You can stand still and look fierce?'

choices.text: Put on the armour

effects.log: You stand still and look fierce for three hours in paste armour. Your neighbours shout your name. You have never been so happy and so itchy.

choices.text: Say no, but carry the props

effects.log: You carry spears, a paper tiger and the emperor's chair. By the end you know the play by heart from behind.

events.arc: A Walk-On at the Temple Fair
events.text: The troupe comes back every year for the fair, and every year {npc} gives you a part one line bigger. This year you have a whole speech: the old general who refuses to retreat.

choices.text: Give the speech

ok.log: You forget nothing. On the last line an old soldier in the crowd stands up and salutes. {npc} hugs you in the wings, covered in your paint.

fail.log: You forget the middle and make up a new one about your vegetable garden. The crowd loves it more. {npc} writes it into the play.

choices.text: Ask for the smaller part again

effects.log: You play the soldier with no lines one more time, and look fiercer than ever. {npc} says you are the only actor who has never been late.

events.arc: A Walk-On at the Temple Fair
events.text: The troupe's wagon comes without {npc} this year. The young troupe master says {npc} retired to a river town and sends you this: the old general's painted mask, the one {npc} wore when young.

choices.text: Wear it in the play once

effects.log: The young actors fall silent when you come on in it. You give the speech in {npc}'s own voice, and know it.

choices.text: Hang it on your wall and go to the river town to visit

effects.log: You find {npc} feeding ducks. 'You came,' {npc} says. 'Say the garden speech. I miss it.'

events.text: On the twenty-third of the twelfth month the Kitchen God goes up to heaven to report on the household. The custom is to smear honey on the paper god's mouth so only sweet words come out. You have run out of honey.

choices.text: Use malt sugar instead

effects.log: The paper god's mouth sticks shut entirely. A neighbour says that is even better: nothing bad, nothing good. A quiet year.

choices.text: Confess the whole year to the paper god before you burn it

effects.log: You tell it everything: the shortcuts, the kindnesses, the cake you ate in secret. Then you burn it. You feel ridiculous and clean.

events.text: That year turned out strangely well. The lane now asks you to do their Kitchen God sendings too, as if you had a knack.

choices.text: Do them all, with a little speech each

effects.log: Forty paper gods with forty speeches. The lane gets a reputation for honesty in heaven. The tax collector is suspicious.

choices.text: Show them how to do it themselves

effects.log: Each house confesses to its own god. The lane is quieter that week, and kinder after.

events.text: New Year's Eve. The Kitchen God comes back down, a fresh paper one pasted on the stove, and this year a child in the lane asks you what he said about you up there.

choices.text: 'That I eat too much honey'

effects.log: The child laughs and tells the whole lane. Next year everyone smears honey on your mouth instead of the god's.

choices.text: 'That I could have done better, and that I will'

effects.log: The child thinks about it seriously. 'Me too,' the child says, and you both shake on it.

events.arc: The Roof in the Plum Rains
events.text: The plum rains have come, a month of warm drizzle, and your roof has found eleven new ways to let it in. The roofer the lane uses, {npc}, is booked until the rains end.

choices.text: Climb up yourself with a basket of tiles

effects.log: You fix four leaks and make two more. {npc}, passing, stops to watch and cannot bear it, and climbs up to help for nothing.

choices.text: Put out every pot you own and live with the music

effects.log: Eleven pots, eleven notes. By the end of the month you can play a tune on them. The neighbours come to listen.

events.arc: The Roof in the Plum Rains
events.text: {npc} has come to do the roof properly, now the rains are over, and keeps stopping to look at the crooked ridge-beam. 'Your house,' {npc} says, 'is older than this street. Look at the joints.'

choices.text: Let {him} take the old roof apart

mem.note: let me open the old roof

effects.log: Under the old tiles is an older roof, and under that a carved ridge-tile of a little lion. {npc} puts it back on top where everyone can see it.

choices.text: Pay for the best tiles (12 taels)

effects.log: Glazed tiles, green as a duck's head. Your roof is the envy of the lane and does not leak for thirty years.

events.arc: The Roof in the Plum Rains
events.text: Thirty plum rains later. {npc} is too old to climb now, and has a grandchild learning the trade, who is standing in your yard looking up at the roof.

choices.text: Let the grandchild practise on your roof

mem.note: let my grandchild learn on that roof

effects.log: Two leaks fixed and one made. {npc} shouts instructions from your bench and you both enjoy it enormously.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to tell the grandchild about the little lion

effects.log: The old roofer tells it like a legend. The grandchild climbs up just to touch the lion for luck.

events.text: A camel caravan bound for the Western Regions is short of hands. Its master, {npc}, a sunburnt person with a voice like gravel, needs someone who can count, cook or walk. 'Three months out, three months back. You will never see so much sky.'

choices.text: Go with the caravan

effects.log: You walk out of the gate behind forty camels with a water skin and a borrowed hat. By the second week your feet have forgiven you.

choices.text: Stay, and send a letter with them instead

effects.log: You write a letter to anyone in the oasis towns who wants one. Months later the caravan brings back an answer from a stranger who keeps bees in the desert.

events.text: A month into the desert. A sandstorm has turned the sky brown, and the caravan has stopped in a ring with the camels kneeling outside. {npc} hands you a cloth for your face. 'Now we wait. Tell me something long.'

choices.text: Tell the story of your whole life so far

mem.note: told me a whole life in a sandstorm

effects.log: It takes the whole storm. {npc} listens, and laughs in the right places, and when the sky clears says, 'Better than most.'

choices.text: Ask {npc} to tell you a story instead

mem.note: listened to the bell city story

effects.log: {npc} tells you about a city under the sand with bells that still ring. You hear them in the wind, or think you do.

events.text: The oasis town at the end of the road: date palms, a blue-tiled well, people from twelve countries arguing over melons. {npc} says the caravan turns back in ten days. 'Some people stay,' {npc} says. 'They say the sky ruins them for walls.'

choices.text: Stay in the Western Regions

effects.log: You watch the caravan go east without you. Then you go and buy a melon, the first of your new life.

choices.text: Go home with the caravan, with a sack of dates

effects.log: Six months later you are back in your own lane, sunburnt, giving away dates. Everyone says you walk differently.

events.text: You need to reach the south, and the cheapest way is a grain barge down the Grand Canal. The bargee, {npc}, sings at the tiller all day, the same three songs, in a voice like a cracked bowl.

choices.text: Take the barge (4 taels)

effects.log: Twelve days of slow water, willows and locks. By the fourth day you are singing the three songs too. By the tenth you have made up a fourth.

choices.text: Work your passage on the ropes

effects.log: You haul the barge through every lock. Your shoulders ache for a month, and in Jiangnan you step off as brown as the bargee.

events.text: Jiangnan: canals instead of streets, bridges every hundred steps, and the rain is soft as breath. You see {npc}'s barge tied up at a water-gate, and {npc} waving a teapot.

choices.text: Spend the day being shown the town from the water

mem.note: saw the town from my barge

effects.log: {npc} knows every bridge by the sound under it. You eat sweet osmanthus cakes at a water-side stall and decide you could live here.

choices.text: Ask {npc} for the fourth song back

mem.note: gave the canal its fourth song

effects.log: {npc} has been singing it up and down the canal. It is famous on the water now, credited to 'a passenger'.

events.text: Years on. A barge comes past wherever you are on the water, and you hear it before you see it: your song, the fourth one, sung by a bargee you have never met.

choices.text: Shout the next line from the bank

effects.log: The bargee nearly drops the tiller. 'You know it?' 'I wrote it.' The bargee does not believe you, and sings it louder.

choices.text: Ask after {npc}

effects.log: 'The old one? Retired to a houseboat at the third lock. Still sings the three songs, badly.' You go and visit, and it is true.

events.text: You have business in Sichuan and stay at an inn whose cook, {npc}, takes your request for 'not too spicy' as a personal insult.

choices.text: Eat what {npc} cooks, as it comes

mem.note: ate my cooking as it came

effects.log: Numbing peppercorns, chilli oil, a fish swimming in red. Your mouth goes numb and then sings. You weep, you sweat, you ask for more.

choices.text: Ask for the plainest dish there is

effects.log: {npc} brings you plain rice with a single, enormous chilli on top, as a warning. You eat around it for a week and then, one evening, bite.

events.text: Before you leave Sichuan, {npc} presses a paper packet into your hand: red peppercorns, the good ones, from {his} own family's terraces. 'Where you come from they cook like the dead. Fix it.'

choices.text: Promise to fix it

effects.log: You carry the peppercorns home wrapped in oilcloth. Your kitchen smells like Sichuan for a year.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to teach you one dish properly first

mem.note: learned the dish under the ladle

effects.log: Three days of lessons. You burn the oil twice and {npc} hits you with a ladle twice. The third time it is right.

events.text: At home, your cooking has become a small scandal. Neighbours complain and come back for more. A child cries at the chilli and then demands it.

choices.text: Plant the last peppercorns in your garden

effects.log: Most die. Three live. Every autumn after that the lane comes to your gate for a handful.

choices.text: Write to {npc}: 'Fixed.'

mem.note: fixed the cooking where they lived

effects.log: A letter comes back months later with another packet and one word: 'Prove it.' You start planning the journey.

events.arc: The First Sight of the Sea
events.text: In all your years you have never seen the sea. A cart is going to the Eastern Coast for salt, and the carter, {npc}, has room for one. 'It is only water,' {npc} says. 'A lot of water.'

choices.text: Go

mem.note: took me to see the sea

effects.log: Six days of road. Then, from a hill, a line of light across the whole bottom of the world. You stand up in the cart and do not sit down for an hour.

choices.text: Not yet: ask the carter to bring back a jar of seawater

effects.log: {npc} brings it back, grumbling. You taste it. It is unbelievably salty. You resolve to go next time.

events.arc: The First Sight of the Sea
events.text: You are on a beach of grey sand, and the sea keeps coming at you and going away again, as if it cannot decide. Fisherfolk mending nets are laughing at you, because you have taken your shoes off and are walking in it like a child. {npc} watches from the cart, eating a pear.

choices.text: Let them laugh and keep walking

effects.log: A wave knocks you down and you come up laughing louder than they are. One of them gives you a shell with the sound of the sea inside.

choices.text: Ask them to take you out in a boat

effects.log: Beyond the breakers the land is a thin line and the sky is enormous. You are sick over the side, twice, and you have never been happier.

choices.text: Decide you are never leaving the coast

effects.log: You rent a room over a net-loft with a window on the water. The carter goes home without you, shaking {his} head.

events.arc: The First Sight of the Sea
events.text: You keep the shell by your bed. A neighbour's child holds it to an ear and hears the sea, and asks if it is real.

choices.text: Tell the child about the beach, every detail

effects.log: The child listens with the shell pressed so hard to one ear that it leaves a mark. Years later you hear the child has gone to the coast.

choices.text: Give the child the shell

effects.log: 'But then you will not hear it.' 'I have heard it,' you say. That is true, and you find it is enough.

events.text: On the Northern Frontier your horse goes lame on the open grass, a day from anywhere. At dusk a herder on a short shaggy horse rides up, looks at your horse and then at you, and says in rough speech: 'Tent. Come.'

choices.text: Follow the herder

effects.log: A round felt tent, a fire of dried dung, a bowl of salted milk tea so strong it could stand up. The herder, {npc}, laughs at the face you make and refills it.

choices.text: Camp where you are out of pride

mem.note: was too proud for the tent

effects.log: A cold, howling night. In the morning {npc} is there again, with a second horse and a look of deep pity.

events.text: You stay with {npc}'s family until the horse heals. The children want to wrestle you; the grandmother wants to know why southerners are all so thin.

choices.text: Wrestle the eldest child

ok.log: You win once, out of five. The whole camp cheers the one. The grandmother gives you a second bowl of mutton.

fail.log: Flat on your back in the grass five times. The children adopt you as a kind of large toy.

choices.text: Help with the sheep instead

effects.log: You are useless with sheep. The sheep know it. But you can mend harness, and by the end every strap in the camp is yours.

events.text: Years later, in your own town, someone is asking at the market for you by a southern name mispronounced in a northern way. It is {npc}, older, with a horse to sell and a felt bag of dried cheese for you.

choices.text: Make {him} the guest this time

mem.note: made me a guest in the south

effects.log: Your house is small and the tea is weak and {npc} is delighted with everything. {He} sleeps in the yard because walls make {him} nervous.

choices.text: Take {him} to the best noodle shop and watch {him} eat

effects.log: Four bowls. {npc} declares southern food 'thin but brave'. You agree to visit the grass again.

events.text: There is a Taoist temple on the sacred mountain, at the top of a stair said to have a thousand steps. Pilgrims climb it once in a life. A fellow pilgrim, {npc}, with a bad knee and a good laugh, falls in beside you at the bottom. 'Count them,' {npc} says. 'Nobody ever agrees.'

choices.text: Count every step

effects.log: You count one thousand and seventy-two. {npc} counts nine hundred and ninety-eight. You argue the whole way down, and are friends by the bottom.

choices.text: Help {him} with the bad knee and lose count

mem.note: gave me an arm up the steps

effects.log: You take {his} arm for the last three hundred. At the top neither of you knows how many steps there were, and it does not matter at all.

events.text: At the top, the temple is small and windy and the old priest is cross about the draught. {npc} asks the priest the one question every pilgrim asks: what is at the top of the mountain?

choices.text: Listen to the answer

effects.log: 'You are,' says the priest, crossly, and shuts the door. {npc} laughs so hard {he} forgets {his} knee.

choices.text: Ask your own question instead

effects.log: 'How many steps?' The priest smiles for the first time. 'Depends who is carrying whom.'

events.text: A letter from {npc}: the knee is worse, and {he} will never climb the mountain again. Would you climb it once more and count, and tell {him} the number?

choices.text: Climb it and count, for {him}

effects.log: Your own knees ache now. You count one thousand exactly, and write it in big characters. {npc} writes back: 'Finally, someone agrees with me.'

choices.text: Write back that the number does not matter

effects.log: {npc} replies at once: 'It does to me.' You laugh and go anyway, and count, and get a third number.

events.arc: The Map of Every Road You Walked
events.text: Clearing out a chest you find, among other things, a pile of old travel notes: inns, rivers, a good tree at a crossroads. You have walked a great deal of the empire without ever drawing it.

choices.text: Start a map on a length of silk

effects.log: Your first attempt puts the river on the wrong side of the mountain. Your second is better. The silk begins to fill with roads.

choices.text: Put the notes back and leave it

effects.log: The notes go back in the chest. Some evenings you find yourself reciting the inns in order, under your breath.

events.arc: The Map of Every Road You Walked
events.text: The map is the length of your arm now. A travelling merchant sees it pinned on your wall and stops dead. 'That ford is marked wrong on every official map. You have it right.'

choices.text: Let the merchant copy it for nothing

effects.log: Within a year three caravans use your ford and nobody drowns at the wrong crossing. A copy of your map is in a magistrate's office.

choices.text: Sell a copy (to gain 20 taels)

effects.log: The merchant pays and is pleased. You use the silver for more silk.

events.arc: The Map of Every Road You Walked
events.text: The map is finished as far as your legs went. There is a blank corner, the far south, where you never walked.

choices.text: Leave it blank and write: 'someone else's'

effects.log: Years later a young traveller asks to fill it in, and does, and sends you the silk back with the south drawn in a different hand.

choices.text: Fill it in from other people's stories

effects.log: Your south is full of things that may not exist. It is the most popular corner of the map.

events.text: A fever takes you in the wet season and does not let go. For nine days the ceiling beams move when you look at them. The herbalist from the market, {npc}, comes with a sack of roots and a face like a closed door.

choices.text: Drink every bitter bowl

effects.log: Bitter, then more bitter, then a kind of bitter you did not know a tongue could hold. On the twelfth day you sit up and ask for rice.

choices.text: Argue about every ingredient

effects.log: You argue from your sickbed about each root. {npc} enjoys it more than {he} will admit and explains them all. You recover knowing more medicine than you meant to.

events.text: You are up but weak, walking the lane with a stick like an old person. Everything looks new: the colour of the persimmons, the shouting of the children, the smell of rain on the dust. {npc} comes to check on you.

choices.text: Tell {him} you see everything differently now

effects.log: {npc} nods. 'Everyone does, for a month. Try to keep some of it.' You try. A little of it stays.

choices.text: Ask to learn which roots grow wild near here

effects.log: {npc} walks you along the river, slowly, pointing. Half of the bitter bowl was growing behind your own house.

events.text: Years later a neighbour's child has the same fever you had, the ceiling-moving kind, and the parents are frightened. {npc} is too old to come out in the rain.

choices.text: Gather the roots yourself from behind your house

effects.log: You get one of them wrong and {npc}, consulted at the window, corrects you. The child sits up on the twelfth day and asks for rice.

choices.text: Sit with the child and tell stories through the worst nights

effects.log: You tell every story you know, twice. The child gets better, and remembers the stories, and none of the fever.

choices.text: Carry {npc} over in a chair under an umbrella

mem.note: carried me through the rain to a sick child

effects.log: {npc} grumbles under the umbrella the whole way and is at the bedside in a moment, closed-door face and all. The child lives.

events.text: You lift a water jar the way you have lifted it ten thousand times, and something in your back goes with a sound like a snapped twig. You lie on the floor of the yard, looking up at a very interesting cloud.

choices.text: Call for help

effects.log: A neighbour hears and fetches the old needle doctor, {npc}, who arrives chewing something and puts six needles in you while you are still talking.

choices.text: Lie there and wait for it to pass

mem.note: lay in the yard an hour first

effects.log: It does not pass. After an hour the neighbourhood cat sits on your chest. At dusk a neighbour finds you and fetches the needle doctor, {npc}, who is not sympathetic.

events.text: Two weeks of needles. {npc} says your back is fine and the trouble is how you stand, sit, walk, lift and sleep, which is to say everything.

choices.text: Learn to stand like a mountain

effects.log: {npc} makes you stand with a bowl of water on your head every morning. You spill it for a month. Then you stop spilling it, and your back stops hurting.

choices.text: Ask for the needles and keep doing everything wrong

effects.log: The needles work for a while. {npc} sighs a great deal and takes your silver for years.

events.text: {npc} is retiring and has nobody to give the needles to. 'You have had more of them in you than anyone,' {npc} says. 'You might as well learn which end goes in.'

choices.text: Learn the needles

effects.log: It takes two winters. You practise on a melon and then on yourself. In the end you can stop a headache in three needles and a bad back in six.

choices.text: Decline, but take the bowl-on-the-head exercise to the lane

effects.log: Every morning a line of neighbours stands in the lane with bowls on their heads. The bonesetter in the next town complains of lost business.

events.text: The world has been going soft at the edges for a year. Now the faces across the street are only colours. A travelling eye doctor at the market says the clouds in your eyes can be pushed aside with a golden needle, or you can learn to live with the mist.

choices.text: Let the eye doctor try the needle (15 taels)

effects.log: A terrifying morning with your head in a vice. Then a week in the dark. Then light, sharp as a knife, and the faces of your neighbours, older than you remembered.

choices.text: Learn to live by ear and hand

effects.log: You learn the lane by its sounds: the cooper's hammer, the hens, the creak of the third step. You know everyone by their footstep before they speak.

events.text: A neighbour's child has taken to leading you to the market by the hand, chattering about everything there is to see.

choices.text: Ask the child to describe everything, exactly

effects.log: The child becomes the best describer in the province: 'a cloud like a fat dog that has given up'. Years later the child writes poems people buy.

choices.text: Teach the child the sounds in return

effects.log: You teach the child to hear which cart has a broken wheel before it comes round the corner. The child is astonished and practises with eyes shut.

events.text: With your new eyes you go round the town, seeing it again. The paint on the temple is faded. The child you once taught to write is a magistrate's clerk. The river is the same.

choices.text: Paint the temple door yourself

effects.log: Your strokes are slow and careful. The red is too bright. The temple keeper says the gods do not mind bright.

choices.text: Sit by the river and just look

effects.log: You look at the river all afternoon, the same water and different. You are not sure which of the two you are.

events.text: Every winter now you have the cough: a deep, rattling thing that wakes the house. This winter it is worse. Your spouse lies awake listening to it.

choices.text: Let your spouse make the pear soup

effects.log: Pears stewed with rock sugar and dried lily bulbs. It does very little for the cough and a great deal for you. You drink it every night.

choices.text: Go to the hot springs in the hills for a month (10 taels)

effects.log: A month of steam and boredom. The cough leaves you somewhere on the hill road. Your spouse says the house is too quiet without it.

events.text: Spring. The cough is gone. Your spouse confesses that through the worst nights, unable to sleep, they started writing down the things you say in your fever.

choices.text: Ask to hear them

effects.log: You said, apparently, that the moon owes you money, that the cat is the emperor, and that you would marry your spouse again every single time. You blush at only one of these.

choices.text: Refuse to hear them, laughing

effects.log: Your spouse reads them aloud anyway, at dinner, with feeling. The neighbours hear through the wall and are very entertained.

events.text: The cough comes back one winter, and this time it is your spouse who has it. You lie awake listening.

choices.text: Make the pear soup

effects.log: You get it wrong: too much sugar, not enough lily. Your spouse drinks every bowl and pretends it is perfect.

choices.text: Write down the fever-talk

effects.log: Your spouse says, in fever, that the dog was right about everything. You keep the page. Neither of you knows what it means.

events.text: You fall off a ladder while picking loquats and break your leg below the knee. The bonesetter ties it to a board and says three months, flat, no arguments. A neighbour's old grandmother sends a whittling knife.

choices.text: Whittle

effects.log: Your first carving is a lump. Your tenth is a duck. By the end of the third month there is a whole wooden farmyard on your windowsill.

choices.text: Read every book in the lane

effects.log: You borrow eleven books, three of them twice. Your leg heals and so does something in your head you had not known was hurt.

events.text: Your leg is mended, slightly crooked, and it tells you the weather two days early. The children of the lane have discovered your wooden farmyard.

choices.text: Give the animals away one by one

effects.log: Every child in the lane has a duck, a pig or an ox. They bring them to you to be mended for years.

choices.text: Sell them at the fair (to gain 6 taels)

effects.log: Six taels and a stall-keeper who wants more. You carve a little every winter after, because your leg likes it.

events.text: A carpenter's apprentice, lame from birth, sees your carvings at a neighbour's house and comes to ask how a person learns to carve lying down.

choices.text: Teach the apprentice

effects.log: The apprentice is better than you inside a year and carves a whole temple of tiny figures. Your duck is in it, at the front.

choices.text: Give the apprentice your old knife

effects.log: The knife has a notch from the first lump. The apprentice keeps it as a charm, and does not use it, and is never without it.

events.text: Another tooth goes, the good one you chewed with. You are now down to the arguing teeth, the ones that only do the talking.

choices.text: Discover tofu

effects.log: Soft tofu, silken tofu, tofu skin, stinky tofu. You become an expert. The tofu seller gives you a discount and a title: Honoured Customer of the Bean.

choices.text: Have a false tooth carved from bone (6 taels)

effects.log: It fits badly and whistles on the letter s. You become famous in the lane for whistling hello.

events.text: The tofu seller is retiring and wants to give the business to a nephew who cannot tell good beans from bad. The tofu seller asks you, the Honoured Customer of the Bean, to judge the nephew's first batch.

choices.text: Judge it honestly

effects.log: It is terrible. You say so, kindly, and then come back every morning for a month to taste the next one. On day thirty it is good.

choices.text: Praise it and quietly teach the nephew afterwards

effects.log: The nephew never knows how bad the first batch was. The tofu gets better, and the nephew gives you a lifetime discount.

events.text: A grandchild in the lane asks why you laugh with your hand over your mouth.

choices.text: Take the hand away and laugh properly

effects.log: The child stares at your gums and laughs too. You both laugh until the tofu seller comes out to see what is wrong.

choices.text: Tell the child the story of each lost tooth

effects.log: The tooth lost to a walnut, the tooth lost to a fall, the tooth lost to a kiss. The child decides teeth are not worth keeping anyway.

events.text: The village has no teacher. The children run wild in the paddies and none can write their names. The abbot of the little temple offers the side hall, if someone will teach.

choices.text: Teach them yourself

effects.log: Twelve children, one broken slate and a pot of water for writing on stone. The first week you teach nothing. The second week a child writes the character for rice and screams with joy.

choices.text: Pay a poor scholar from town to come (10 taels)

effects.log: The scholar is shy and good. You sit at the back, and learn as much as the children.

events.text: One pupil, a fisher's child named Little Pebble, is always last in and first out, and never says a word, and is the only one who has learned every character you have taught.

choices.text: Give Little Pebble the old book of poems

effects.log: Little Pebble takes it without a word, holding it like an egg. Next morning the child recites the first poem in a voice like a bell.

choices.text: Ask why the child runs off so early

effects.log: Little Pebble has to mend nets for the family's boat every afternoon. You move the lessons to the morning. The whole class does better.

events.text: A sedan chair stops at your gate. Out steps a county official in blue, who bows to the ground in front of your house. It takes you a long moment to see Little Pebble in the face.

choices.text: Bow back, just as low

effects.log: You both bow so low that neither of you can get up. The bearers have to help. You laugh for an hour over tea.

choices.text: Ask if the official still mends nets

effects.log: 'Every spring,' says Little Pebble, 'for the family boat.' The official builds the village a proper schoolhouse with a net-mending room.

events.text: Every summer someone's child goes into the river too deep. This year it was nearly the miller's youngest. You can swim, and almost nobody in the village can.

choices.text: Start teaching the children to swim

effects.log: Ten children in the shallows, kicking. You hold each one up by the belly. Mothers stand on the bank with their hearts in their mouths.

choices.text: Rope off the deep part with floats

effects.log: A rope of gourds across the river. It does not stop anyone, but everyone knows where the deep part starts now.

events.text: Your swimmers have grown. Some of them teach the little ones now. This summer the river floods higher than anyone remembers and a cart is swept off the ford.

choices.text: Go in with your oldest swimmers

effects.log: You and three young people you taught to kick bring the carter out between you. The carter coughs up half the river and asks who taught you all.

choices.text: Stand on the bank and direct

effects.log: You shout where the current turns. Your swimmers do the rest, neatly, the way you taught. You have never been prouder of anything.

events.text: An old swimmer now, you still go in on the first hot day. The children of your first swimmers line the bank and wait to see whether the old one will make it across.

choices.text: Swim across

ok.log: Slowly, steadily, all the way. They cheer as if you had won a war. You lie on the far bank in the sun.

fail.log: Halfway, your arms decide otherwise, and three of the children are in the water at once to tow you back, kicking beautifully.

choices.text: Wade to your waist and teach the new ones from there

effects.log: You stand in the water like a heron, holding up bellies. It is the same as it was forty years ago.

events.text: In summer the children of the lane gather on your step at dusk because you once told them a story about a tiger who was afraid of chickens. Now they want another, every night.

choices.text: Tell them a new one every night

effects.log: Tigers, ghosts, a clever ferry girl, a dragon who could not swim. You run out of stories by midsummer and start making them up.

choices.text: Teach them to tell their own

effects.log: Each child tells one. They are terrible and wonderful. A small one tells a story with no ending, just a cat, and everyone loves it.

events.text: Years later at the market you overhear a young parent telling a child your tiger story, wrongly: in this telling the tiger is afraid of ducks, and it is set in the parent's own village.

choices.text: Correct the story

effects.log: The parent stares at you. Then: 'You are the one from the step.' You both sit on a bench and argue about ducks.

choices.text: Leave it: the ducks are better

effects.log: You walk on, smiling. Stories are like children: they leave and become whatever they become.

events.text: A collector of folk tales from the capital comes through your town, and keeps hearing the same stories, with ducks or chickens, with a ferry girl or a ferry boy. All of the trails lead to your step.

choices.text: Tell the collector the true first versions

effects.log: The collector writes them down exactly. In the book they are 'tales of the region, origin unknown'. You find that you prefer it that way.

choices.text: Tell a brand new one, for the book

effects.log: The collector is delighted and you are delighted. It is the best story you ever told, and the last.

events.text: Your nails keep vanishing from the workshop shed, a few at a time. One evening you catch the thief: a thin child from the docks with a bag of them, building a boat out of driftwood behind the wall.

choices.text: Ask the child to show you the boat

effects.log: It is very bad and very brave. You show the child how a hull should curve. Next week the child is back, and you leave the shed unlocked.

choices.text: Take the nails back and give the child a hammer

effects.log: The child stares at the hammer. 'It's not stealing if you have the hammer?' 'It's not stealing if you ask.'

events.text: The dock child has been in your shed every evening for two years. The boat is finished: small, tarred, leaky, perfect. The child wants to launch it on the river.

choices.text: Launch it together

effects.log: It floats. It leaks. The child bails with both hands and laughs and rows to the far bank and back. Half the docks watch.

choices.text: Tar it once more first, properly

effects.log: One more evening of work, together. It does not leak at all, and the child learns that the last coat is the one that counts.

events.text: A fishing boat with a new hull ties up at your landing. Its owner, a weather-brown adult with a careful smile, hands you a small bag. It is full of nails.

choices.text: Laugh and invite the visitor in

effects.log: You talk until the lamp is out about hulls and rivers. The visitor's own child is waiting in the boat, holding a hammer.

choices.text: Ask to go out on the boat

effects.log: The hull is good, the curve is the one you once showed a child. You sit in the bow and say nothing for an hour, which says everything.

events.text: A fortune-teller at the temple gate reads your palm for one copper and says, cheerfully, that you are exactly halfway through your life. Then asks what you have done with the first half.

choices.text: Make a list that night

effects.log: The list is shorter than you hoped and longer than you feared. At the bottom you write: 'second half'. You stare at it until the lamp runs out.

choices.text: Laugh and buy the fortune-teller a bun

effects.log: The fortune-teller eats the bun and says, with a full mouth, that the second half is usually better. 'People stop asking permission.'

events.text: The list from the night after the fortune-teller is still in your drawer. One line on it has been bothering you: 'never learned to do anything just for myself'.

choices.text: Learn to paint birds

effects.log: Your birds look like potatoes with opinions. You paint them every evening anyway and become unreasonably happy.

choices.text: Walk to the next province, alone, for no reason

effects.log: Nine days out, nine days back. You come home with no souvenirs and a face that people keep asking about.

choices.text: Cross the line out and write 'still deciding'

effects.log: It is the most honest line on the list. You keep the list and add to it for the rest of your life.

events.text: You pass the temple gate and the fortune-teller waves you over, as if you were old friends. 'The second half,' the fortune-teller says. 'Have you stopped asking permission yet?'

choices.text: 'Yes'

effects.log: 'Liar,' the fortune-teller says happily, and gives you the bun back, so to speak: a fortune for nothing. It says you will live long and argue well.

choices.text: 'Not yet. Tell me how'

effects.log: 'Do one thing a year that nobody asked you to do.' That year you plant a plum tree by the road. Nobody asked.

events.text: At an inn you meet {npc}, who grew up two villages from yours, and who, at the age you once nearly left home to wander the jianghu, actually did. {npc} has a scar, a sword {he} cannot sell, and a lot of stories.

choices.text: Ask whether it was worth it

mem.note: asked me if it was worth it

effects.log: {npc} thinks a long time. 'Some days. I envy you the house. You envy me the road. Neither of us is right.' You drink to that.

choices.text: Tell {him} about your life instead

effects.log: {npc} listens hungrily to the ordinary details: the roof, the neighbours, the market days. 'That,' {npc} says, 'is the adventure I never had.'

events.text: {npc} turns up at your door a year later. 'I want to try your life,' {he} says. 'For a month. Show me how to be ordinary.'

choices.text: Teach {him} to mend a roof and haggle for cabbages

mem.note: showed me how to be ordinary

effects.log: {npc} is terrible at both and loves it. On the last day {he} sits on your step and cries a little over a bowl of rice.

choices.text: Swap: {he} teaches you a little of the road

mem.note: swapped lives with me for a month

effects.log: {npc} shows you how to read a stranger's hands and when to leave an inn by the back. You never need either, and are glad to know them.

events.text: {npc} has settled at last, in a house of {his} own at the end of your lane, and is a hopeless gardener, and very happy.

choices.text: Help with the garden

effects.log: Your two gardens become one long, quarrelsome garden. You grow the cabbages; {npc} grows the stories.

choices.text: Ask whether the road was better after all

effects.log: 'The road was the road,' {npc} says. 'This is better because I came back to it.' {He} hands you a cabbage with a worm in it.

events.text: Washing your face in the basin, you see it: a grey hair, bold as a thread of silver, right at the front.

choices.text: Pull it out

effects.log: Two grow back in its place, by the custom of grey hairs everywhere. You declare a truce.

choices.text: Leave it and show everyone

effects.log: You point it out to the whole lane. The lane points out theirs. It becomes a contest. The baker wins.

choices.text: Ask an herbalist for black-sesame paste
