effects.log: A month of black-sesame paste. The hair stays grey. You develop a lifelong love of black-sesame paste.

events.text: Your hair is half grey now and the children call you 'the badger'. One of your old friends, meeting you after years, does not recognise you at the market.

choices.text: Introduce yourself formally, like a stranger

effects.log: Your friend plays along. You meet each other all over again over tea, and it is just as good the second time.

choices.text: Say: 'You are no young willow either'

effects.log: You both laugh until the market looks round. Then you count each other's grey hairs, and lose count.

events.text: White, now, all of it. In the market a young person helps you down a step, and you realise with a jolt that you have become the old one in the lane.

choices.text: Accept the arm with grace

effects.log: You accept, and say thank you, and the young person glows. Being helped, you find, is a thing you can give.

choices.text: Hop the next step to prove a point

effects.log: You hop it, wobble, and are caught. The young person laughs and so do you. 'Next year,' you say, 'I will hop two.'

events.text: You have always loved the guqin, the old seven-string zither of scholars. A blind teacher, {npc}, takes pupils in a room above the rice shop. Every pupil there is under fifteen.

choices.text: Climb the stairs anyway

mem.note: came up the stairs at fifty

effects.log: You sit among the children with your knees around your ears. The children are kind to you, in the way of children: completely honest about your playing.

choices.text: Ask for private lessons at dawn (5 taels)

effects.log: Dawn lessons, alone. {npc} listens to your first note for a long time and says only: 'Again.' You play it again for a year.

events.text: Two years of lessons. Your fingers hurt and your playing has become merely bad. {npc} says it is time to learn a real piece: 'Flowing Water', which every player spends a lifetime on.

choices.text: Try to play it all the way through

ok.log: You get through it. It is clumsy, but in the middle there is one passage that is really water. {npc} turns {his} face toward it and smiles.

fail.log: You stop five times. {npc} says, 'Good. Now you know how long a lifetime is.'

choices.text: Play only the first phrase, over and over, until it is right

effects.log: A whole winter on one phrase. When you finally play it right, the children downstairs stop their noise to listen.

events.text: {npc} is very old now and the lessons have stopped. You climb the stairs above the rice shop with your own guqin under your arm.

choices.text: Play 'Flowing Water' for {him}

mem.note: played me the water at last

effects.log: Your playing is still not good. But the water is there, now, all through it. {npc} listens with {his} eyes shut and does not say 'again'.

choices.text: Play the first phrase, the one from that winter

effects.log: {npc} laughs. 'That one. You were so stubborn.' Then {he} asks you to play it again, and again.

events.text: One morning you notice how quiet the house has become. Fewer feet, fewer voices. Even the kettle seems to have lowered its voice.

choices.text: Get a cat

effects.log: The cat is called Magistrate, after its manner. It knocks things off shelves and the house is not quiet again.

choices.text: Invite the lane in for dinner once a month

effects.log: The first dinner is three people. By the sixth it is fourteen, and someone always brings a dish nobody can identify.

choices.text: Sit with the quiet and get to know it

effects.log: It has its own sounds: the eaves, the well chain, your own breathing. You find you are good company.

events.text: A traveller is caught by the rain at your gate and asks for a corner for the night. Your house is quiet and there is a spare room.

choices.text: Give them the room, and a meal

effects.log: The traveller is a seller of combs who talks the whole evening, and leaves you a comb carved like a fish. Your house remembers the voice for weeks.

choices.text: Give them the room, and leave them in peace

effects.log: In the morning there is a swept yard and a note: 'Thank you for the quiet.' You understand it exactly.

events.text: You have kept the spare room ready ever since the comb seller. Travellers seem to know. There has been one most months for years.

choices.text: Hang a sign: 'A quiet house. A bed.'

effects.log: It becomes known on the road. Strangers bring news, recipes, and once a goose. You never charge, and are never short of anything.

choices.text: Keep it as it is, a secret of the road

effects.log: The travellers who find it are the ones who need it. You collect their stories in a book.

events.text: You have given up most of your work and taken up a vegetable garden. A rabbit has taken up your vegetable garden.

choices.text: Build a fence

effects.log: The rabbit digs under it. You dig the fence deeper. The rabbit digs deeper. You are both very fit by summer.

choices.text: Plant extra for the rabbit

effects.log: A row for the rabbit, at the end. The rabbit ignores it and eats your row. You have learned something about the world.

events.text: Year two of the rabbit war. You now know the rabbit's habits better than your neighbours'. It has a torn ear and you have named it General Zhang.

choices.text: Set a clever trap with a box and a carrot

effects.log: General Zhang eats the carrot and leaves the box. You admire the General enormously.

choices.text: Sit very still in the garden at dawn to watch

effects.log: General Zhang comes within an arm's length and eats a lettuce, looking you in the eye. You have never felt so understood.

events.text: General Zhang has not come for a week. Then you find a nest under the gooseberries: four small rabbits, one with a torn ear like its mother's.

choices.text: Plant more lettuce

effects.log: Five rabbits now. Your garden is a rabbit kingdom with a small vegetable district. The neighbours bring their children to watch.

choices.text: Move the nest gently to the hedge outside

effects.log: The rabbits move back in a week. You give up and plant more lettuce, which was always going to happen.

events.text: Retired, you have discovered the teahouse. Its best seat is the corner by the window, where the light is good and the gossip passes. It belongs, by long custom, to {npc}, who has sat there every morning for twenty years.

choices.text: Take the next seat and say good morning

effects.log: {npc} ignores you for a week, then shares the newspaper sheet, then the opinions. You are a pair by spring.

choices.text: Arrive earlier and take the corner

effects.log: {npc} arrives, stops, looks at you in the corner seat. The whole teahouse holds its breath. {npc} sits down opposite you and says, 'Well.'

events.text: You and {npc} are now the teahouse's two old fixtures, and argue every morning about everything: the price of tea, the weather, the magistrate, whether pigeons have souls.

choices.text: Lose an argument on purpose

mem.note: let me win about the pigeons

effects.log: You concede the pigeons. {npc} is suspicious all day. The next morning {he} concedes the weather.

choices.text: Start a rule: whoever loses pays for the tea

effects.log: You pay for the tea for three months straight. Then you discover {npc}'s weak spot, which is fish, and the tea is free for a year.

events.text: {npc} is not in the corner seat this morning. The teahouse keeper says, gently, that {npc} died in the night. The corner seat sits empty in the good light.

choices.text: Leave the seat empty for a month

effects.log: Nobody takes it. The keeper puts a cup of tea there every morning. On the thirtieth day you sit in it, and you can see the whole street.

choices.text: Sit in it now and say {npc}'s side of today's argument

effects.log: You argue both sides about the price of tea. The teahouse listens, and laughs, and cries a little, and pays for your tea.

events.arc: The Bird That Would Not Sing
events.text: Every morning the retired folk of the town carry their songbirds in cages to the park and hang them in the willows to sing together. You buy a lark from the market. It does not sing. It looks at you.

choices.text: Carry it to the park anyway

effects.log: Your lark sits silent among forty singing birds. The old bird-keepers are very sympathetic and give you a great deal of advice, all of it different.

choices.text: Take it back to the bird seller

effects.log: The seller swears it sang in the shop. You keep it out of pity, and buy a second bird that does sing, so the first has a teacher.

events.arc: The Bird That Would Not Sing
events.text: A year of mornings in the park with a silent lark. The other keepers have started a pool of advice for it: millet with honey, a covered cage, a song whistled at dawn.

choices.text: Try the whistled song

effects.log: You whistle every dawn. The lark watches with interest. The neighbours do not. One morning the lark whistles your song back, badly, like an echo of you.

choices.text: Open the cage door in the park

effects.log: The lark hops out onto your finger, sits there, and does not fly. You carry it home on your finger, through the whole town.

events.arc: The Bird That Would Not Sing
events.text: Your lark has become famous in the park: the only bird in town that sings a human's tune, badly. People come from other towns to hear it.

choices.text: Teach it a second tune

effects.log: It refuses. One tune is enough for any bird. The park agrees.

choices.text: Let the young keepers whistle to it too

effects.log: Soon the lark sings three people's tunes, all badly. The park is happier than it has been in years.

events.text: In the square at dawn, old people write huge characters on the flagstones with brooms dipped in water. The characters dry and vanish in minutes. One of them, {npc}, holds out a spare broom.

choices.text: Write your own name

effects.log: Your name, as big as a door, in water. It is gone before you have finished the last stroke. You find you do not mind.

choices.text: Watch {npc} write a whole poem

effects.log: {npc} writes a poem about plums down the length of the square, and the first line is gone before the last is done. Nobody ever reads all of it but the writer.

events.text: You are a dawn calligrapher now. You and {npc} have a friendly rivalry over who can write the longest poem before the first character dries.

choices.text: Write faster than {npc}

mem.note: wrote forty before the first dried

ok.log: Forty characters before the first one dries. {npc} applauds with the broom and splashes everyone.

fail.log: Your broom slips and writes a puddle. {npc} declares the puddle the best character of the morning.

choices.text: Write slower and better

effects.log: One poem, slowly, while the sun comes up. {npc} stops writing to read it before it goes. That is the prize.

events.text: {npc} has died. On the morning after the funeral, you write {his} name in water across the whole square, the largest characters anyone has ever written there.

choices.text: Watch it dry

effects.log: Stroke by stroke the name goes, the way everything goes. The other calligraphers stand with their brooms and wait until it is gone.

choices.text: Write it again as it dries, all morning

effects.log: You write it over and over until the sun is high and the stones are hot. It dries every time. You write it every time.

events.text: Your house has become too much: the stairs, the well, the roof. Your grown child, {npc}, says you should come and live with the family. There is a room at the back that gets the morning sun.

choices.text: Go, and bring only one cart of things

effects.log: One cart. You sort a lifetime into keep and give, and give away almost everything. The room at the back is bright and small and fits you.

choices.text: Stay in your house a while longer

effects.log: {npc} sighs and sends a grandchild round every day to fetch your water. The grandchild steals your persimmons. You both pretend not to notice.

events.text: Living in {npc}'s house has its rules, and none of them are yours. The household eats late, sweeps oddly and keeps the salt in the wrong jar.

choices.text: Keep your opinions to yourself

effects.log: It nearly kills you, but the household notices, and one day your child moves the salt to the right jar, without a word.

choices.text: Take over the cooking one night a week

effects.log: One night a week the house eats your food, the old way. The grandchildren call it Old Night and fight over the last dumpling.

events.text: The household has grown around you, and {npc} has grey hair now. Your grandchildren come to your room in the morning sun to do their lessons, because you never tell them to hurry.

choices.text: Teach them the things nobody else will

effects.log: How to whistle through a leaf, how to tell a ripe melon, how to lose a game gracefully. They will use the last one most.

choices.text: Just sit with them and doze

effects.log: You doze in the sun while they work. Sometimes you wake to find a small hand holding your sleeve.

events.text: There were five of you who grew up running the same paddy dikes. Now, every spring, the five meet at the wineshop by the old granary: you, {npc}, and three others who still tell the same story about the stolen goose.

choices.text: Tell the goose story again

effects.log: You tell it, and are interrupted four times, and the goose grows larger. {npc} laughs until the wine comes out of {his} nose.

choices.text: Propose you write the goose story down

mem.note: wrote the goose story with us

effects.log: It takes all five of you and all evening, and nobody agrees on anything, and the final version has three endings.

events.text: Spring at the wineshop. There are four of you this year, and then, two springs later, three. The innkeeper still sets five cups out of habit, and nobody, least of all {npc}, tells the innkeeper to stop.

choices.text: Fill the empty cups too

effects.log: Five cups filled, three drunk. At the end of the night you pour the other two into the granary ditch, where the goose once ran.

choices.text: Tell the story of the ones who are gone

effects.log: Each of you tells one thing about the missing two that the others did not know. It turns out one of them was the one who stole the goose.

events.text: Spring, and only you and {npc} are left. {npc} is frail now and is carried to the wineshop in a chair. 'Two of us,' {npc} says. 'We should finally agree on the ending.'

choices.text: Agree on the ending

effects.log: You agree that the goose won. It is the truest ending. {npc} weeps with laughter and makes the innkeeper write it on the wall.

choices.text: Refuse, as you always have

effects.log: 'Never,' you say. {npc} grins with all of {his} three teeth. 'Good. Then we have to meet again next year.'

events.text: {npc} has died. At the funeral you are the only one left of the five. The innkeeper comes, carrying five cups on a tray, and gives them all to you.

choices.text: Go to the granary ditch and pour them all

effects.log: Five cups into the ditch, one after another. A goose on the far bank hisses at you, and you laugh, alone and not alone.

choices.text: Keep the five cups on your shelf

effects.log: Five cups in a row. When children ask, you tell them the goose story, the whole thing, with every ending.

events.arc: What to Say at the Grave
events.text: An old friend has died: {npc}'s spouse, a loud, generous person who once lent you a cart and never let you forget it. {npc} asks you to speak at the funeral.

choices.text: Speak of the generosity

effects.log: You speak of the cart, and of all the other carts, figurative and real. Half the mourners were lent something too. They nod and weep.

choices.text: Speak of the loudness, and make them laugh

effects.log: You tell how the dead one once shouted a pig back into its pen from a mile away. The mourners laugh, guilty, then grateful. {npc} laughs the hardest.

events.arc: What to Say at the Grave
events.text: {npc} is living alone now, in a house built for two, and has stopped coming to the market.

choices.text: Go every week with something to mend

effects.log: A chair, a pot, a basket. {npc} mends them, scolding you for breaking everything. It keeps both of you going through the first year.

choices.text: Bring {him} to the market with you

effects.log: {npc} comes, reluctantly, and haggles over a fish, and wins, and for a moment looks like the old self.

events.arc: What to Say at the Grave
events.text: {npc} comes to your gate in good clothes. 'When it is my time,' {he} says, 'I want you to speak. Same as before. Make them laugh.'

choices.text: Promise, and ask what to say

effects.log: You spend the afternoon collecting {npc}'s funny stories from {npc}. Many are about you. You both laugh until the light goes.

choices.text: Say: 'You will have to outlive me, then'

effects.log: {npc} shakes a finger at you. 'We will see.' You are both still arguing about it ten years later.

events.text: At the funeral of a neighbour, the hired mourners arrive in white and begin wailing beautifully. They have come to the wrong house. The right house is two streets away, and has no mourners.

choices.text: Quietly redirect them

effects.log: You walk them two streets over. The other family is overwhelmed with gratitude. The first family pretends not to have noticed the silence.

choices.text: Let them finish, then send them on

effects.log: They wail for both houses, one after the other, and charge for one. The whole town hears of it and considers it a bargain.

events.text: The chief of the hired mourners, an old professional with a voice like a temple bell, comes to thank you and stays for tea. 'Thirty years of weeping for strangers,' the mourner says. 'Do you know who weeps for us?'

choices.text: Ask the mourner to tell you about the work

effects.log: It is a craft, with its own songs, and its own pride, and its own secret: the best mourners think of someone they really lost.

choices.text: Say that you will, when the time comes

effects.log: The mourner laughs and then does not laugh. 'I will hold you to that.'

events.text: Word comes that the old mourner has died. The mourners' guild will sing, but there is no family. You remember the promise.

choices.text: Weep for the mourner, for real

effects.log: You think of everyone you ever really lost. The guild, professionals all, falls silent to listen. They say afterward it was the best weeping in years.

choices.text: Pay for a proper stone (8 taels)

effects.log: A good stone, with the words 'wept for strangers'. The guild sweeps it every Qingming after.

events.text: {npc}, an old friend from your working years, has buried a spouse of forty years, and has stopped cooking. You find {him} eating cold rice out of the pot.

choices.text: Cook for {him}, every evening for a month

mem.note: cooked for me after the funeral

effects.log: You cook badly, and {npc} criticises every dish, which is how you know {he} is coming back.

choices.text: Teach {him} to cook

mem.note: taught me to cook at sixty

effects.log: {npc} has never cooked in {his} life. The first dish is a disaster and makes {him} laugh for the first time in weeks.

events.text: {npc} now cooks one dish very well: pork braised in soy and star anise, the dish {his} spouse loved. {He} wants to cook it for the whole lane on what would have been their anniversary.

choices.text: Help carry the tables out

mem.note: carried the tables for the anniversary

effects.log: Twenty neighbours at long tables in the lane. {npc} serves the dish and tells a story about the spouse with every bowl.

choices.text: Ask what else the spouse loved

effects.log: {npc} makes a list: braised pork, chrysanthemums, bad opera, rain on the roof. You both decide to have all of it.

events.text: {npc} has made the anniversary dinner a custom. This year, at the end of it, {npc} stands up to make a speech, and says that next year {he} would like you to cook.

choices.text: Cook the braised pork, carefully

effects.log: It is not as good as {npc}'s. {npc} says it is better. That is the only lie {he} ever told you.

choices.text: Cook a dish from your own life instead

effects.log: Your own dish, from your own griefs. {npc} eats it slowly and nods. The dinner becomes a night for everyone's lost.

events.text: The stream on the way to market floods every spring and the stepping stones go under. Old people turn back. Children get wet to the waist. Nobody builds a bridge, because nobody owns the stream.

choices.text: Pay for timber and build one with the neighbours (15 taels)

effects.log: A plank bridge on stone piers, crooked and strong. On the first market day the whole village crosses it twice for fun.

choices.text: Build it yourself, slowly, one plank at a time

effects.log: One plank a week. People start leaving planks at your door. By autumn there is a bridge, and you did not pay for half of it.

events.text: The spring flood this year is the worst in twenty years. In the morning the village goes down to the stream to see if your bridge has gone.

choices.text: Go down with them

effects.log: It is still there, battered, one plank missing, the water an arm below it. Somebody starts cheering and then everybody is.

choices.text: Stay in bed: it stands or it does not

effects.log: It stands. They come up to tell you, a whole crowd at your gate, as if you had done something brave.

events.text: The village has carved a name on the bridge post: yours. Children call it by your name without knowing you are a person and not just a bridge.

choices.text: Tell the children who you are

effects.log: They do not believe you. You are much too old to be a bridge. They are right, probably.

choices.text: Keep quiet and cross it every day

effects.log: Every morning you cross yourself on the way to market. It is the best joke of your old age, and only you are in on it.

events.arc: A Tree for People You Will Never Meet
events.text: There is an old saying: a ginkgo planted by the grandfather is picked by the grandson. Ginkgos take thirty years to fruit. You buy a sapling at the market and look at it.

choices.text: Plant it at the edge of the village square

effects.log: Everyone tells you that you will never see the fruit. You say that is not the point. You are not entirely sure what the point is.

choices.text: Plant it in your own yard

effects.log: It is a stick with three leaves. You water it every morning. It is the most hopeful thing you own.

events.arc: A Tree for People You Will Never Meet
events.text: The ginkgo is taller than you now. A goat has eaten one side of it, and it has grown lopsided and stubborn, which you approve of.

choices.text: Build a fence round it

effects.log: A fence of woven bamboo. The goat, insulted, eats the fence. The tree grows on.

choices.text: Teach a neighbour's child to look after it

effects.log: The child waters it, talks to it, and is outraged at the goat. The child will be the one who picks the fruit.

events.arc: A Tree for People You Will Never Meet
events.text: Autumn, and the ginkgo has turned. For a single week every leaf is pure gold, like the tree is lit from inside. Then, overnight, every leaf falls at once.

choices.text: Sit under it in the gold

effects.log: You sit in a drift of gold leaves the morning after. You will never see the fruit. You see this.

choices.text: Show the child, now grown, the gold

effects.log: The child, half grown, stands under it with you and is silent for a very long time. 'I will plant one too,' the child says.

events.text: You realise one evening that the dishes you cook have no book, only you. The braised fish, the pickled turnips, the soup for colds. When you go, they go.

choices.text: Start writing them down

effects.log: It is harder than it looks. 'A little salt' is not a measurement. You start weighing everything, and are astonished at what you actually do.

choices.text: Teach them to a young neighbour instead

effects.log: The neighbour cooks along with you for a winter and learns it the way you did: by hand, not by book.

events.text: The recipe book is thick now. You have reached the soup for colds and find you do not remember who taught it to you, only the taste.

choices.text: Write 'from someone kind' at the top

effects.log: It is the truest attribution in the book. You start writing it on others too.

choices.text: Ask the old people of the lane if they know it

effects.log: Three of them do, each a little differently. You write all three versions down, and the book becomes the lane's.

events.text: A young cook, about to leave for the city, asks to copy your recipe book.

choices.text: Give the book itself

effects.log: 'But then you have none.' 'I have the hands,' you say. Years later a city restaurant serves 'soup from someone kind'.

choices.text: Copy it out by hand together, over a winter

effects.log: Two books. The young cook argues with your measurements and is usually right. You make corrections in your own copy.

events.text: You have begun thinking about who gets what when you are gone. There is not much: a few books, a quilt, and a little clay teapot so old the clay has drunk thirty years of tea and makes any water taste of it. Everybody wants the teapot.

choices.text: Decide now, and tell everyone

effects.log: You announce it at dinner: the teapot goes to whoever brews the best pot of tea before then. A silent war of brewing begins.

choices.text: Say nothing and let them work it out

effects.log: Your relatives start bringing tea round, very attentive. You have never drunk so much good tea in your life.

events.text: The tea war has gone on for two years. Every caller now brings a better tea than the last. One quiet neighbour's child has brought nothing but has listened to every story you told over the cups.

choices.text: Give the teapot to the quiet child, now

effects.log: The relatives are outraged for a day, then laugh. The child brews you the worst tea you have ever drunk, in the best teapot, and you drink all of it.

choices.text: Declare a winner among the tea-bringers

effects.log: You choose the one whose tea made you laugh: a jasmine so strong it smelled like a wedding. The others sulk and keep visiting anyway.

events.text: Your teapot has a new home, and you drink from a cheap new pot that tastes of nothing. The one who has the old teapot comes every week and brews it for you.

choices.text: Say it tastes just the same

effects.log: It tastes better, because someone carried it over. You do not say that part.

choices.text: Start seasoning the new pot

effects.log: Thirty years of tea, starting now. You laugh at yourself and brew the first pot. Someone, someday, will want it.

events.text: The village is putting up a stone by the shrine with the names of everyone who has lived past seventy. The village head comes round to ask how you want your name carved.

choices.text: Just the name

effects.log: Your name, plain, among others. You go and look at it at dusk, and it looks back.

choices.text: The name and one word

effects.log: You think about the word for a week. In the end it is 'tried'. People stop and read it and nod.

choices.text: Ask that a neighbour's name be added who died at sixty-nine

effects.log: The village head hesitates, then carves it with a little mark: 'nearly'. The neighbour's family weeps and thanks you.

events.text: A schoolchild has been sent to copy the names on the Elders Stone for a lesson, and has stopped at yours, and found you sitting by it.

choices.text: Tell the child your life in one breath

effects.log: One breath: a place, a few loves, some work, a lot of rice. The child writes it down exactly. It sounds like a poem.

choices.text: Ask the child which name they like best

effects.log: The child picks a name you knew: a terrible cook who was always kind. You tell the child about the cooking, and the kindness.

events.text: Spring. Someone has planted flowers around the Elders Stone, a different colour by each name. Yours is blue.

choices.text: Find out who planted them

effects.log: It was the schoolchild, older now. 'Blue, because you said blue things are calm.' You do not remember saying it. It sounds like you.

choices.text: Water them all, every morning

effects.log: It becomes your walk. You water every name. Some of them, you water twice.

events.text: {npc} brings the youngest of the grandchildren to visit, a small serious person who has never flown a kite, and who stares at the sky as if it were a locked door.

choices.text: Build a kite together, from scratch

effects.log: Bamboo, paper, rice-paste, string. Your grandchild paints a face on it with enormous teeth. It flies, wobbling, over the threshing floor, and the serious face splits into a grin.

choices.text: Buy a fine kite at the market (3 taels)

effects.log: A swallow kite with a long tail. Your grandchild holds the string as if it were alive and will not let anyone else touch it.

events.text: Spring wind. {npc} brings your grandchild back, taller now, and the grandchild wants to fly the kite higher than the temple roof. Somehow it has become your job to make that happen.

choices.text: Let out all the string and run

ok.log: Higher than the temple roof, higher than the crows. Your grandchild screams with joy. You sit down in the grass, out of breath and very pleased with yourself.

fail.log: You trip over a furrow and the kite goes into the temple's pine. Your grandchild climbs up to fetch it and you both get told off by the abbot.

choices.text: Show how to read the wind first

effects.log: You teach your grandchild to watch the grass and the smoke and the birds. The kite goes up on the first try, and your grandchild looks at you as if you knew magic.

events.text: Your grandchild is grown now and has a small child of their own, who has never flown a kite, and who stares at the sky as if it were a locked door. {npc}, grey now, laughs at the sight.

choices.text: Watch your grandchild teach it

effects.log: You sit on the bench and watch your grandchild do everything you did, including the mistakes. The kite goes up. Two generations grin at you.

choices.text: Bring out the old kite with the painted teeth

effects.log: It is yellow and torn and your grandchild cries at the sight of it. You mend it together and it flies once more, wobbling, over the same threshing floor.

events.text: {npc} has left a grandchild with you for the afternoon. The grandchild has reached the age of questions. 'Why is the sky blue? Why do old people have spots? Why did you not become a general?'

choices.text: Answer every question honestly

effects.log: 'I do not know. Because we are old. Because I did not want to.' Your grandchild considers the answers and finds them all satisfactory.

choices.text: Answer every question with a story

effects.log: The sky is blue because a dragon spilled dye. Spots are where the years land. You were going to be a general, but there was a duck. Your grandchild demands the duck story.

events.text: {npc} leaves the grandchild with you again, and the grandchild has a new question, the kind that comes with growing: 'Were you ever afraid?'

choices.text: Tell the truth about one fear

effects.log: You tell about a winter when you were very afraid, and what you did. Your grandchild listens without moving, and afterwards holds your hand on the way home.

choices.text: Say 'Every day, a little', and laugh

effects.log: Your grandchild laughs too, relieved. 'Me too.' You agree to be a little afraid together.

events.text: Your grandchild, grown, comes to visit and sits where they used to sit as a child, and says: 'I have a question I never asked.'

choices.text: 'Ask it'

effects.log: 'Were you happy?' You think about it for a long time, honestly. Then you say yes, mostly, and it is true, and your grandchild smiles in exactly the way {npc} did at that age.

choices.text: 'Let me ask one first'

effects.log: You ask whether they are happy. The answer is long and complicated and good. You never get round to the other question, and it does not matter.

events.text: A red invitation: your eldest grandchild is to marry in the spring. {npc} writes that the family hopes you will sit in the place of honour, and that you are absolutely not to make a speech.

choices.text: Promise not to make a speech

effects.log: You promise. You start preparing a speech that night, in secret.

choices.text: Insist on a short one

effects.log: {npc} sends back a letter that is mostly sighing. You are allowed thirty words.

events.text: The wedding feast. Firecrackers, red lanterns, the whole family. Your grandchild bows to you before the couple bows to anyone else. The room goes quiet.

choices.text: Say thirty words

effects.log: You count them on your fingers under the table. Twenty-nine, then the last word: 'Eat.' The room roars and eats.

choices.text: Say nothing, only take both their hands

effects.log: You hold their hands and cannot speak at all. It turns out to be the speech everyone remembers.

choices.text: Give the secret speech after all

effects.log: It is four pages long. {npc} puts {his} head in {his} hands. By page three the whole hall is crying with laughter.

events.text: Your grandchild and the new spouse come to visit you, shy and grown-up, carrying a gift: a little scroll with your thirty words, or your silence, or your four pages, written out in fine calligraphy. {npc} has come too, to watch your face.

choices.text: Hang it by your bed

effects.log: You read it every morning. It is the best thing you ever said, or did not say.

choices.text: Ask them to tell you how they met

effects.log: It takes all afternoon and they disagree on every detail. You recognise the argument. It is a good sign.

events.text: Your grandchild, on the edge of being grown, takes you aside in the orchard. 'Do not tell {npc}. I want to leave. To see the jianghu. Everyone says it is dangerous and stupid.'

choices.text: Ask what they hope to find there

effects.log: Your grandchild talks for an hour, and none of it is about fighting. It is about roads and strangers and finding out who they are. You listen to the end.

choices.text: Tell them a true story of the road

effects.log: You tell them of a bad night at an inn and a good stranger the next morning. Your grandchild hears both halves, which is the point.

events.text: {npc} has found out, and is furious, and comes to you because your grandchild says you knew.

choices.text: Take your grandchild's side

effects.log: {npc} does not speak to you for a month. Then {he} comes back and says, 'You let me go, once.' You had forgotten. {npc} had not.

choices.text: Help them find a middle road: one year, with letters

effects.log: One year, a letter every month. Your grandchild agrees, {npc} agrees, and both of them think they won.

events.text: A letter, months late, from the road. Your grandchild is well, has been robbed once and helped twice, and has learned to cook rice over a fire. At the end: 'Tell {npc} I am coming home in the spring. Not for good. To visit.'

choices.text: Read it to {npc} aloud

effects.log: You read it twice. The second time {npc} laughs at the part about the rice, and {his} shoulders come down for the first time in a year.

choices.text: Write back with every bit of news from home

effects.log: Your letter is six pages: the dog, the roof, the pear tree. In the spring your grandchild comes home and knows everything already.

events.text: {npc} comes up the path carrying a bundle, followed by a grown grandchild. The bundle is your first great-grandchild. There are four generations in your yard.

choices.text: Hold the baby

effects.log: The baby looks at you with enormous dark eyes, then grabs your nose very hard. Everyone laughs. You do not let go for an hour.

choices.text: Ask for a portrait of the four of you (5 taels)

effects.log: A travelling painter sits you all in a row. In the painting you all look stiff and frightened, except the baby, who is asleep.

events.text: The great-grandchild can walk now, mostly sideways, and has decided that you are the most interesting person alive, because you move as slowly as it does. {npc} watches the two of you from the step.

choices.text: Race it across the yard

effects.log: You lose, narrowly, on purpose, then not on purpose. Four generations cheer from the step.

choices.text: Show it the ants

effects.log: You sit together on the ground and watch a line of ants carry a grain of rice. For a whole hour neither of you needs anything else.

events.text: You have started writing down your life, in the evenings, on cheap paper. It comes out in the wrong order. The things you thought were important take one line. A dog you had for a year takes four pages.

choices.text: Let it come in the wrong order

effects.log: You write what comes. The book is crooked and true. You stop worrying whether anyone will read it.

choices.text: Hire a young scribe to help (6 taels)

effects.log: The scribe is nineteen and has opinions about your sentences. You argue every evening. The book gets better, and so do the arguments.

events.text: You have reached the hard chapter: the one with the thing you did that you are not proud of. You have been circling it for weeks.

choices.text: Write it plainly

effects.log: You write it in plain words and read it back. It is smaller on paper than it was in you. You sleep well that night for the first time in a long while.

choices.text: Leave it out

effects.log: You leave it out. The book has a gap in it, and you can feel exactly where. You decide that is the truest page of all.

events.text: The memoir is finished: one thick, uneven book. You have to decide what to do with it.

choices.text: Give it to the person who will need it most

effects.log: You give it to a young neighbour about to make the same mistake you made at that age. Weeks later the neighbour comes back, saying nothing, and bows.

choices.text: Have it copied for the temple library (10 taels)

effects.log: It sits on a shelf between a sutra and a book of herbs. A monk tells you it is borrowed more than either.

choices.text: Wrap it and put it away for whoever finds it

effects.log: You wrap it in oilcloth and put it in the rafters. Somebody, someday, will find it and laugh at the dog chapter.

events.arc: The Young Scholar With the Notebook
events.text: A young scholar from the capital, {npc}, is going from village to village writing down how old people lived: what they ate in famine years, what songs they sang at planting. {npc} asks whether you will talk.

choices.text: Talk, for days

effects.log: You talk about the famine, the songs, the price of salt in the year of the comet. {npc} fills three notebooks and runs out of ink.

choices.text: Make {him} work in your field while you talk

effects.log: {npc} weeds your field with blistered hands and writes in the evening. The notes are better for it.

events.arc: The Young Scholar With the Notebook
events.text: {npc} has come back with a question: three old people have told the same story about the great flood, and in all three you are in it, doing something different.

choices.text: Tell what really happened

effects.log: The truth is smaller than any of the stories: you held a lantern on the dike all night so others could see. {npc} writes it down and calls it the best version.

choices.text: Say all three are true

effects.log: {npc} laughs and writes them all down. 'Folk memory,' {he} says. 'The best kind of lie.'

events.arc: The Young Scholar With the Notebook
events.text: A parcel from the capital: {npc}'s book, printed, with a page about your village. Your name is not in it. Your lantern on the dike is.

choices.text: Read the page aloud at the wineshop

effects.log: Everyone listens. Everyone recognises their own small part. Nobody's name is in it and everybody is.

choices.text: Write {npc} a thank-you letter, with one more story

effects.log: You send the story of the stolen goose, or a duck, or a ferry. {npc} writes back: second edition.

events.text: Under a loose floorboard you find a little sewn book in your own handwriting, younger and rounder: a diary from when you were about nineteen.

choices.text: Read it all, cringing

effects.log: You were very sure about everything. You were going to be famous. You were in love three times in one spring. You laugh until your stomach hurts.

choices.text: Read only the last page

effects.log: The last page says: 'Tomorrow I will start being who I am.' You sit with that for a long time.

events.text: There is a promise in the diary you made yourself at nineteen: to learn to swim, or see the capital, or plant a pear tree. You never did.

choices.text: Do it now, decades late

effects.log: You do it, slowly and badly and completely. Then you write it in the diary, under the promise, in your old handwriting: 'Done. Sorry it took so long.'

choices.text: Write a reply to your younger self

effects.log: A long letter to a nineteen-year-old who will never read it. You tell them it all turned out differently, and fine.

events.text: A young person in your lane is nineteen, very sure of everything, and in love three times this spring.

choices.text: Give them a blank book

effects.log: 'Write it all down,' you say. 'You will want it later.' They roll their eyes and take it, and you see them writing in it on the step.

choices.text: Read them one page of yours

effects.log: They are horrified and delighted. 'You were like this?' 'Worse.' You become, against all expectation, someone they trust.

events.text: You wake one morning knowing, simply, that you want to see the place you were born once more. It is a long way, and your legs are not what they were.

choices.text: Go on foot, slowly, the way you left

effects.log: A walking stick, a bundle, a hat. You take three times as long as you would have once, and see three times as much.

choices.text: Hire a cart and a driver (8 taels)

effects.log: The driver is young and chatty and asks about everything. By the end you have told the driver your whole life, and the driver has told you theirs.

events.text: The village is smaller than you remembered, and also bigger. The old well is still there. The house you were born in has a different roof and children you do not know playing in the yard.

choices.text: Knock and tell them you were born here

effects.log: The family is delighted and gives you tea in the room where you were born. The children ask whether the house was haunted then too.

choices.text: Stand at the gate and do not knock

effects.log: You look for a long time. A child waves at you. You wave back. That is enough.

choices.text: Go to the old well and drink from it

effects.log: The water tastes exactly the same. You are seven again for the length of a swallow.

events.text: On the road home you stop at a crossroads inn, and realise you no longer know which home you mean. Both are. Neither is.

choices.text: Go home to where you live

effects.log: You come back to your own door, your own bed, your own neighbours, who say you look different. You do. You came all the way round.

choices.text: Stay a night longer at the inn and tell your story to strangers

effects.log: Three travellers listen to your life by the fire. In the morning one of them is walking the other way, toward where you were born.

events.arc: Down the River One More Time
events.text: {npc}, a friend of fifty years, turns up with a plan: one last trip down the river on a hired boat, the way you both went as young people when you had nothing and the river was free.

choices.text: Go

effects.log: A slow boat, a jug, two old people under an awning. The banks go by. You recognise a tree you climbed half a century ago.

choices.text: Say you are too old, then go anyway

effects.log: You complain for the first mile and are silent with joy for the next twenty.

events.arc: Down the River One More Time
events.text: Night on the river. The boatman sleeps at the stern. {npc} wants to say something important and keeps not saying it.

choices.text: Wait for it

mem.note: heard the thank-you on the river

effects.log: Toward dawn {npc} says it: thank you, for everything, plainly. You say it back. Then you both pretend you were talking about the fish.

choices.text: Say it first

mem.note: said it first on the river

effects.log: You say it, and {npc} laughs, relieved, and says, 'I have been trying for an hour.'

events.arc: Down the River One More Time
events.text: Back home, {npc} gives you the jug from the boat, empty, with a stopper. 'For the next trip,' {npc} says. You both know there will not be one.

choices.text: Keep it on your windowsill

effects.log: The jug sits in the window and catches the morning light. Every time you see it, you are on the river.

choices.text: Fill it with river water and give it back

effects.log: {npc} laughs and keeps it on {his} windowsill. When {npc} dies, years later, the jug comes back to you, still full.

events.text: You have not spoken to your cousin {npc} in twenty years, over something said at a funeral that neither of you can quite remember now. Today you see {him} across the market, buying the same kind of pear you buy.

choices.text: Walk over and buy the pear next to {his}

mem.note: came and stood at the pears

effects.log: You stand side by side choosing pears and saying nothing. Then {npc} says, 'Those are bruised.' It is the first thing in twenty years.

choices.text: Send a pear round to {his} house, with no note

effects.log: The next day a pear comes back, with no note. Then nothing for a month. Then another pear.

events.text: You and {npc} are now on pear terms. But neither has mentioned the funeral. It sits between you like a third person at the table.

choices.text: Ask what was actually said

effects.log: Neither of you can remember. You piece it together: something about a hat. You both laugh until you cry, and then just cry a little.

choices.text: Apologise anyway, for whatever it was

effects.log: {npc} looks at you for a long moment. 'Me too,' {he} says. 'For whatever it was.'

events.text: {npc} has a confession: there is a whole branch of the family who were not spoken to because of the same hat. Children who never met their cousins. A whole wedding nobody went to.

choices.text: Throw a pear feast for every branch

effects.log: Forty relatives, many of whom have never met. Somebody brings up the hat, and a great-aunt confesses to having worn it. The feast goes on until dawn.

choices.text: Visit the branches one by one with {him}

mem.note: walked the family round with me

effects.log: A winter of visits, with pears. Some doors open and some do not. More open than shut.

events.text: The old village teacher who used to rap your knuckles with a bamboo cane is still alive, very frail, and living alone. {npc} sits in the doorway every morning and nobody visits.

choices.text: Visit, once, out of curiosity

effects.log: {npc} does not recognise you, then does. 'You. The one who wrote the characters backward.' {He} still has the cane. It is a walking stick now.

choices.text: Walk past, as you always have

effects.log: You walk past. The next morning you walk past again, more slowly. On the third morning {npc} calls your name.

events.text: You have taken to visiting {npc}. Today {he} asks, out of nowhere: 'Was I cruel to you?'

choices.text: Tell the truth: 'Sometimes'

effects.log: {npc} nods slowly. 'I was afraid you would not learn. I was afraid of a great many things.' You sit together in the doorway and the sun comes round.

choices.text: Say: 'You taught me to write my name'

effects.log: It is true, and it is not the whole truth, and {npc} knows it, and is grateful for it anyway.

events.text: {npc} asks you to read to {him}, because {his} eyes are gone. The book is the primer {he} taught you from.

choices.text: Read it, and get one character wrong on purpose

effects.log: {npc} lifts the cane, then laughs, the first laugh you have ever heard from {him}. 'Backward,' {he} says. 'Still.'

choices.text: Read it perfectly

effects.log: You read it perfectly. {npc} listens to the end and says only, 'Good.' It is the word you waited for as a child.

events.arc: The Friend Who Did Not Come
events.text: {npc} was your closest friend once, and did not come to the most important day of your young life, and never said why. Now a letter arrives in {his} handwriting, after all these years.

choices.text: Open it

effects.log: It is short. {npc} was ashamed: no money for a gift, no good clothes, and too proud to come without. {He} asks if you will meet {him} at the old bridge.

choices.text: Leave it unopened for a month

effects.log: A month on the shelf. Then you open it on a sleepless night and read it twice.

events.arc: The Friend Who Did Not Come
events.text: The old bridge. {npc} is there, older, in clothes that are clearly the best {he} owns, holding a small wrapped package: the gift {he} never gave.

choices.text: Open the gift there on the bridge

effects.log: It is a wooden comb, carved years ago, never given. It is beautiful. You cannot speak for a while, and neither can {npc}.

choices.text: Say none of it ever mattered

mem.note: let it matter, then let it go

effects.log: {npc} shakes {his} head. 'It mattered to me.' You stand on the bridge and let it matter, and then let it go.

events.arc: The Friend Who Did Not Come
events.text: {npc} is a friend again, as if the years had folded shut. This year, at a feast of your house, {npc} is the first to arrive, in good clothes, carrying a gift far too expensive.

choices.text: Scold {him} for the gift

effects.log: 'I owed you one,' {npc} says. 'With interest.' The whole feast hears about the comb, and the bridge.

choices.text: Sit {him} at your right hand

mem.note: sat me at the right hand

effects.log: The place of honour. {npc} is mortified and delighted. It is the first time {he} has been anywhere first.

events.text: For a week, the little temple bell on the hill has rung once at midnight. The monks say they are asleep. The village says ghosts. You cannot sleep anyway.

choices.text: Climb up and watch

effects.log: At midnight a shape in a grey robe comes out of the trees, rings the bell once, and goes back. You follow, as quietly as you can.

choices.text: Ask the old abbot directly

effects.log: The abbot looks at you a long time. 'Come at midnight,' the abbot says. 'Bring tea.'

events.text: It is the abbot, ninety years old and unable to sleep, who has been ringing the bell because the monk who used to ring it at midnight, forty years ago, was the abbot's oldest friend, and died this week a year ago.

choices.text: Keep the secret

effects.log: You tell the village it was an owl. Every midnight for the rest of that year you hear the bell and smile in the dark.

choices.text: Offer to ring it for the abbot

effects.log: Every midnight for a month you climb the hill and ring it once. The abbot sleeps, finally, and thanks you with a pot of temple tea.

events.text: The abbot has died. The village is at the funeral. At midnight, without anyone asking, the bell rings once.

choices.text: Go up and see who

effects.log: A young monk, red-eyed, holding the rope. 'The abbot told me the story,' the monk says. 'Someone has to.'

choices.text: Stay in bed and listen

effects.log: One ring. You lie in the dark with your eyes open. Someone always remembers.

events.text: After the first snow you find footprints on your roof: small ones, going right across the ridge from the neighbour's side to the street side, and then nothing, as if whoever made them had flown.

choices.text: Sit up the next snowy night to watch

effects.log: At the fourth watch a small shape crosses your roof, very light-footed. In the morning there are new footprints, and a sweet bun on your step.

choices.text: Put a bowl of rice on the roof

effects.log: In the morning the bowl is empty and there is a pebble in it, polished, like a thank-you.

events.text: The roof-walker is a child from the poor street, who has been crossing the roofs every night to take food to a sick grandmother on the other side of town, because the streets are not safe after dark.

choices.text: Walk the child through the streets with a lantern instead

effects.log: Every night for a winter. The child talks the whole way. The grandmother recovers, and makes you shoes.

choices.text: Leave a better path: a plank between your roof and the next

effects.log: The child is delighted. The neighbours never notice. Your roof becomes the first stop on a secret road.

events.text: Years later the roof-walker comes to see you, grown and quick-footed still, wearing a messenger's badge for the post road. 'I cross the whole province now,' they say. 'Your roof was the start.'

choices.text: Ask them to deliver one letter for you

effects.log: A letter to someone far away whom you have not written to in years. It arrives in record time.

choices.text: Ask them to walk your roof one more time

effects.log: They do, laughing, light as a cat, in broad daylight, and the whole lane comes out to watch.

events.text: The rice cakes left on the little earth-god shrine at the end of the lane are vanishing every night. The lane is divided: a fox, a ghost, or the earth god finally getting hungry.

choices.text: Hide behind the shrine and watch

effects.log: Cramped, cold, and patient. At midnight a very old dog with one ear comes, takes one cake, looks right at you, and leaves.

choices.text: Leave a better cake, to see if the taste is particular

effects.log: The better cake vanishes faster. The worse cake stays. The thief has standards.

events.text: The thief is an old one-eared dog nobody owns, who has been living under the shrine. The lane wants it chased off.

choices.text: Speak up for the dog

effects.log: You say the earth god chose a guardian. The lane, half joking, agrees. The dog gets a bowl of its own beside the shrine.

choices.text: Take the dog home yourself

effects.log: The dog walks into your house as if it had always lived there and takes the best place by the stove.

events.text: The old dog has died, very old, asleep. The lane holds a small ceremony at the shrine, half joking, and nobody's eyes are dry.

choices.text: Carve a little stone dog for the shrine

effects.log: It sits by the earth god forever, one ear carved, and children pat its head for luck.

choices.text: Keep leaving a cake out

effects.log: Every night, one cake. Some nights it vanishes. You decide not to find out why.

events.arc: The Jar Under the Plum Tree
events.text: Digging a hole for a new plum tree, your spade hits something: a sealed clay jar, very old. Inside, wrapped in waxed cloth, are a handful of old coins and a letter.

choices.text: Read the letter

effects.log: It is a letter to a child, from a parent going away to a war long ago: 'If you find this, I did not come back, but I meant to.' The child's name is on it.

choices.text: Take it to the village elders first

effects.log: The elders read it and fall silent. The name on the letter is one of the village's old families.

events.arc: The Jar Under the Plum Tree
events.text: You find the family: one old person left, the grandchild of the child the letter was written to. The old person never knew the great-grandparent's name, only that someone went to war and did not come back.

choices.text: Give them the letter and the coins

effects.log: The old person reads the letter a dozen times. 'He meant to,' they say. 'He meant to come back.' They light incense for him for the first time in a hundred years.

choices.text: Read it to them, slowly

effects.log: They listen with their eyes shut. When you finish they ask you to read it again. You read it until you know it by heart.

events.arc: The Jar Under the Plum Tree
events.text: The old family has asked you to plant the plum tree after all, over the place where the jar was. 'He would want something to grow there,' they say.

choices.text: Plant it together

effects.log: A small plum tree, two old hands and yours. It flowers the next spring, early, white.

choices.text: Bury a new jar under it first

effects.log: You write a letter to whoever finds it in a hundred years, and seal it in the jar. You do not tell anyone what you wrote.

events.text: In the window of a pawnshop hangs an old portrait of a stranger in clothes from a century ago, who looks exactly like you. Not a little like you. Exactly.

choices.text: Buy it (6 taels)

effects.log: The pawnbroker is very happy to see it go. 'Customers kept saying it looked at them.' At home it hangs opposite the door and you nod to it each morning.

choices.text: Ask the pawnbroker where it came from

effects.log: From the estate of a family on the hill road, long ago. The pawnbroker gives you the name of the village.

events.text: You go to the village on the hill road. The old people stare at you, and one of them drops a basket.

choices.text: Ask who you look like

effects.log: The face is that of a doctor who lived there a hundred years ago and treated everyone for nothing. The village still sweeps that grave.

choices.text: Laugh and say you are not a ghost

effects.log: They laugh too, eventually. Then they feed you, just in case, and tell you the doctor's whole life.

events.text: You have taken the portrait to the village on the hill road, where it hangs in the shrine. Whenever you visit, the children argue about which of you is which.

choices.text: Learn a little medicine, to live up to it

effects.log: You learn some herbs and a few needles. Nothing grand. Enough that once or twice a year you are useful on the hill road.

choices.text: Let the children decide

effects.log: The children decide you are the doctor's grandchild a hundred times removed, and treat you with enormous ceremony. You enjoy it.

events.text: A ginger cat has adopted you. It eats your fish, sleeps on your quilt, and is called Pumpkin. Then you hear the noodle-seller calling it Commander, and the widow at the well calling it Little Treasure.

choices.text: Confront the noodle-seller

effects.log: You and the noodle-seller compare notes. The cat eats a full dinner at each of three houses. You both admire it.

choices.text: Feed it less, to see what happens

effects.log: It eats more at the other two houses. The widow tells everyone you are cruel to cats.

events.text: The three households have formed an alliance: the cat is fed only once a day, in turns. The cat has noticed and is offended.

choices.text: Hold firm

effects.log: The cat finds a fourth house. The alliance gives up. The cat grows enormous and sleeps on the warmest roof in the lane.

choices.text: Break the alliance in secret with a little fish

effects.log: The cat chooses you, on your quilt, every night. You never tell the others. They never tell you about their little fish.

events.text: The ginger cat is old now and moves slowly between its houses. One evening it stays on your quilt and does not get up to go to the others.

choices.text: Send word to the other two houses

effects.log: The noodle-seller and the widow come and sit with you. Three people and a cat on a quilt, all night. It goes peacefully, purring, with all its names.

choices.text: Sit up with it alone

effects.log: You stroke it until dawn and call it all three names. In the morning the other two houses come to ask, and you bury it together.

events.text: On the hill above the river stands a tall rock the village calls the Waiting Stone: a woman, they say, who waited so long for a boat that never came that she turned to stone. Every child knows the story. Nobody knows her name.

choices.text: Ask the oldest people in the village

effects.log: Five old people, five different names, and one who says the stone was a man, waiting for a woman, and the village changed it because it sounded better.

choices.text: Climb up and look at the stone properly

effects.log: Up close it is just a rock, weathered and lichened. But from the top you can see exactly as far down the river as anyone waiting could.

events.text: In the county records, in a box nobody has opened in a century, you find it: a ferry keeper's wife who kept a lamp lit on that hill every night for thirty years, so the night boats could find the landing. Her husband came home every time.

choices.text: Tell the village the true story

effects.log: Half the village prefers the old story. The other half starts lighting a lamp on the hill on festival nights.

choices.text: Keep both stories

effects.log: You tell the children both, and let them choose. Most choose the lamp. The romantic ones choose the stone.

events.text: A night boat, lost in fog on the river, finds the landing by the lamp on the Waiting Stone, which someone has lit tonight for no festival at all.

choices.text: Go down to meet the boat

effects.log: The boatman is shaking. 'There was a light,' the boatman says, 'on the rock.' You both look up at it. Thirty years, a hundred years: still burning.

choices.text: Go up the hill to see who lit it

effects.log: Nobody is there. Just the lamp, full of oil, and a new name scratched at the foot of the stone: the ferry keeper's wife's, at last.

events.text: In the temple pond lives a tortoise the size of a cart wheel, said to be three hundred years old. There are characters carved on its shell, worn nearly smooth.

choices.text: Make a rubbing of the shell

effects.log: You lie on the pond's edge with paper and charcoal while the tortoise ignores you. The rubbing shows a date and a name: a scholar who freed it, two centuries ago.

choices.text: Feed it a lotus leaf and wait

effects.log: It eats the leaf in a single bite and looks at you with deep, unbothered patience. You find you are calmer the whole day.

events.text: A merchant has offered the temple a fortune for the tortoise, for a rich man's garden. The monks are poor, and the roof leaks.

choices.text: Raise money for the roof instead (10 taels)

effects.log: You give what you can and go round the town. The roof is mended and the tortoise stays, and does not notice either.

choices.text: Tell the merchant about the scholar who freed it

effects.log: The merchant listens, embarrassed, and withdraws the offer, and pays for the roof himself, for the luck.

events.text: You are old now, and the tortoise is exactly the same. You sit at the pond's edge and think that it will still be here when you are not.

choices.text: Carve your own name on a little stone by the pond

effects.log: One small name beside a three-hundred-year-old one. It seems the right size.

choices.text: Say goodbye to it, just in case

effects.log: The tortoise blinks at you, slowly, once. You decide that it means something, and you are probably right.

events.text: On the hill path there is a shrine to the fox spirit the size of a birdhouse. Most people walk past it. Some people leave a little wine, and swear their luck improves.

choices.text: Leave wine every month

effects.log: Your luck does not obviously improve. But you stop losing things, which is a kind of luck.

choices.text: Fix its broken roof

effects.log: It takes an afternoon. The next morning there are fox prints all round it, and one on your doorstep, which is three miles away.

events.text: A wild fox has started appearing at the edge of your yard at dusk, sitting very still, watching you work.

choices.text: Leave out a bowl of water

effects.log: Every evening the bowl is empty. You never see the fox drink. The neighbours start calling you the fox's friend, half joking.

choices.text: Talk to it while you work

effects.log: You tell it about your day. It listens, or seems to. One evening it brings you a single shiny button, and leaves it on the step.

events.text: You have been the fox shrine's keeper, unofficially, for many years. A child asks you whether the fox spirit is real.

choices.text: 'Something is'

effects.log: The child nods seriously. The next month the child brings wine for the shrine, and a button.

choices.text: Take the child up to fix the roof together

effects.log: You teach the child how to set a tile. The fox prints are on your doorstep the next morning, both sets.

events.text: The inn on the north road is said to be haunted: at the fourth watch a figure in white walks the corridor and opens every door. Travellers avoid it. The innkeeper, {npc}, is going broke.

choices.text: Stay the night and see

effects.log: At the fourth watch your door opens. A figure in white looks in, says 'Good, all asleep,' and shuts it again. You follow.

choices.text: Lend {him} some money to tide over (5 taels)

effects.log: {npc} is grateful and embarrassed and swears the ghost is harmless. You go back to find out what that means.

events.text: The ghost is {npc}'s grandmother, who is ninety-four and sleepwalks, and spent sixty years as the inn's night-keeper checking that every guest was safe.

choices.text: Suggest {npc} advertise it

mem.note: saved my inn with a sign

effects.log: 'The Inn of the Watchful Grandmother. Your sleep is guarded.' Travellers come from three provinces. The grandmother is delighted.

choices.text: Help {npc} hang bells on the grandmother's door

effects.log: Little bells, so the family wakes at every midnight walk. The grandmother is led back to bed every night, scolding, and the inn is quiet.

events.text: The grandmother has died, at a hundred. Travellers swear that the corridor is still walked at the fourth watch, and that their doors open, and close again, gently.

choices.text: Stay the night once more

mem.note: came back for the last watch

effects.log: At the fourth watch your door opens a crack and closes. Nobody is in the corridor. You sleep better than you have in years.

choices.text: Ask {npc} if it is true

effects.log: {npc} smiles. 'I walk it now,' {he} says. 'Someone has to check.'

events.text: High on the mountain lives a hermit nobody has spoken to in decades. Once a month the village leaves a sack of rice at the foot of the last cliff, and once a month it is gone.

choices.text: Carry the rice up this month

effects.log: At the cliff's foot there is an empty sack from last month, folded neatly, with a carved wooden spoon on top.

choices.text: Leave a note with the rice

effects.log: You write: 'Is there anything else you need?' Next month the sack is gone, and there is a note in its place: 'Salt. And news.'

events.text: You have been carrying the rice for a few years, and writing a page of news with each sack: who married, who died, what the river did. The hermit writes back one line each time.

choices.text: Ask the hermit's name

effects.log: The reply: 'I have forgotten it. Give me one.' You give the hermit a name, and it is used to sign every note after.

choices.text: Ask why the hermit left

effects.log: The reply comes after two months: 'Too much news.' You laugh until you have to sit down on the rice.

events.text: This month the sack from last month is still there, untouched. The rice has not been taken.

choices.text: Climb the last cliff to see

ok.log: At the top is a tidy hut and a garden and the hermit, very old, very ill, and very surprised. You carry the hermit down to the village, where the hermit dies a month later, warm, among neighbours, and asks for news every day.

fail.log: You get halfway and can go no further. You shout news up the cliff until your voice gives out. A spoon drops down to you, carved with your name.

choices.text: Leave the rice and a longer note than ever

effects.log: You write ten pages. The next month, the rice is gone and so are the pages, and there is no reply, and you understand it.

events.text: In the public bathhouse there is an old regular, {npc}, who sits in the hottest pool every afternoon and explains the universe to whoever will listen. Today that is you.

choices.text: Listen

effects.log: {npc} explains that the world is a pot of soup and that people are the dumplings, rising when done. You think about it for a week.

choices.text: Argue

effects.log: You argue that people are the noodles, not the dumplings. The whole bathhouse joins in. Nobody leaves for two hours and everyone comes out red as a crab.

events.text: {npc} has a new theory: that the soul is the steam. {He} wants to test it by sitting in the hottest pool longer than anyone has ever sat.

choices.text: Talk {him} out of it

mem.note: talked me out of the steam test

effects.log: {npc} agrees to test it by thinking about it instead, which {he} admits is more {his} sort of experiment.

choices.text: Time {him} with a water clock

effects.log: Half an hour. {npc} comes out the colour of a lobster, triumphant, and faints in the cold room. The soul, {he} says on waking, is not the steam.

events.text: {npc} is too frail now for the hot pool and sits on the bench at the side, dangling {his} feet in the water, still talking.

choices.text: Bring the new young regulars over to listen

effects.log: The young ones think {npc} is mad and come back every day. The bathhouse has a philosopher again, and soon two.

choices.text: Ask {him} the last question: what is the soup?

mem.note: asked about the soup at last

effects.log: {npc} thinks a long time. 'Everything that is not you,' {he} says. 'Be a good dumpling.'

events.text: The barber at the bridge, {npc}, shaves faces with a razor sharp enough to split a hair and talks without stopping. By the time {he} is done you know every scandal in the district.

choices.text: Become a regular

effects.log: Once a fortnight. {npc} tells you everything, and you learn that a barber's chair is the safest place in town to hear the truth.

choices.text: Say nothing at all, to see what happens

effects.log: {npc} is so unnerved by your silence that {he} tells you {his} own secrets instead. You keep them.

events.text: {npc}'s hands have begun to shake. The razor trembles at your throat. {npc} has noticed, and is frightened, and keeps talking to cover it.

choices.text: Keep coming, and tell {him} you trust {him}

effects.log: You sit very still. The shave is slow and perfect. {npc} puts the razor down afterward and does not talk for a whole minute.

choices.text: Suggest {he} teach an apprentice and just talk

effects.log: A young apprentice holds the razor; {npc} sits beside the chair and talks. Business doubles. Talking was always the trade.

events.text: {npc} has retired to a stool beside the bridge, where people stop to hear the news. {He} asks to shave you once more, the last shave.

choices.text: Sit for it

effects.log: {His} hands are steady for the whole shave, as if they had been saving it. Afterward {npc} folds the razor and gives it to you.

choices.text: Shave {him} instead

effects.log: You are terrible at it and {npc} talks you through every stroke. It is the best conversation you have ever had with a razor at someone's throat.

events.text: A government clerk is going house to house for the census, writing down everyone's name, age and trade. The clerk asks your age.

choices.text: Tell the truth

effects.log: The clerk writes it down without looking up. You feel oddly recorded, as if you had been pinned to a board.

choices.text: Knock off five years

effects.log: The clerk looks up, looks at you, and writes down the real number anyway. 'Everyone does it,' the clerk says. 'I add them back.'

events.text: Ten years on, the same clerk, much older, comes for the next census, and remembers you, and asks what has changed.

choices.text: Tell all of it

effects.log: The clerk has no column for most of it. The clerk writes it in the margin anyway, very small.

choices.text: Ask what has changed for the clerk

effects.log: Nobody has ever asked. The clerk sits down on your step and talks for an hour, and leaves the census unfinished for the day.

events.text: The census again. A young clerk this time. The old one, the young clerk says, has died, and left a note in the margin of the ledger next to your name: 'asked about me.'

choices.text: Ask to see the old ledger

effects.log: In the margins of thirty years of censuses, in small writing, are the lives that did not fit the columns. You read them for an afternoon.

choices.text: Tell the young clerk to write in the margins too

effects.log: The young clerk looks startled, then thoughtful. 'Is that allowed?' 'It is now.'

events.text: The young couple next door are marrying, and both families, who have been feuding about a drain for three generations, insist that you, the neutral neighbour, give the toast.

choices.text: Toast to the drain

effects.log: You raise a cup 'to the drain, which has brought these families closer than anything'. There is a silence. Then the grandfathers laugh at the same moment.

choices.text: Keep it short and sweet

effects.log: Two lines and a raised cup. Everyone drinks. Nobody fights. You consider it a triumph.

events.text: The drain between the two families has blocked again, as it does every spring, and both grandfathers are standing over it, glaring.

choices.text: Hand each of them a shovel

effects.log: They dig it out together, grumbling. By the end they are arguing about something else entirely, which is progress.

choices.text: Fix it yourself while they argue

effects.log: You are knee-deep in mud before they notice. Both families are so ashamed that they fix the drain properly, together, the next week.

events.text: The young couple's first child is named after the drain, more or less: a name meaning 'flowing water'. Both grandfathers claim credit.

choices.text: Laugh until you cry

effects.log: You laugh for a full minute. The grandfathers laugh too, eventually. The child will never know why everyone smiles at its name.

choices.text: Give the child a toy boat for the drain

effects.log: The child sails it down the drain every spring. Both families watch from either side.

events.text: Thirty years married, near enough. Your spouse says they want nothing for the day. You have been married thirty years and know exactly what that means.

choices.text: Recreate the first meal you ate together

effects.log: You get half of it wrong and your spouse corrects you on every dish. The corrections are the best part.

choices.text: Give nothing, as asked

effects.log: Your spouse is outraged, then laughs, then admits wanting a new teapot. You had already bought it. It was hidden in the woodpile.

events.text: Your spouse has a confession, years overdue: the thing you most argued about in your first year, they were wrong, and knew it, and could not say.

choices.text: Confess one of your own

effects.log: You confess the broken jar you blamed on the cat. Your spouse laughs so hard that the neighbours come to see.

choices.text: Say you knew all along

effects.log: 'You knew?' 'Thirty years.' Your spouse looks at you with something you have not seen in a while, and it is very good to see.

events.text: Forty years married. You sit on the step in the evening, not needing to talk. The cat, the fourth or fifth cat of the marriage, sits between you.

choices.text: Hold hands

effects.log: Old hands, spotted and creased. They still fit. You sit until the stars come out.

choices.text: Start the old argument, for fun

effects.log: You both know your lines by heart. You both get the laughs in the right places. The cat leaves in disgust.

events.text: Your spouse has started to snore. It is a deep, rattling, wall-shaking snore, the snore of a tiger with a head cold, and your spouse denies it completely.

choices.text: Prove it: wake them mid-snore

effects.log: Your spouse wakes, says 'I was not snoring,' and is asleep and snoring before finishing the sentence. You lie awake laughing.

choices.text: Buy a herbal pillow for it (3 taels)

effects.log: The pillow smells of chrysanthemum and does nothing. You both sleep on it anyway, for years, because it smells nice.

events.text: You have discovered, from a neighbour over the wall, that you also snore. Loudly. In harmony.

choices.text: Confess it to your spouse

effects.log: Your spouse is triumphant for a week. Then you both agree to a truce, and the neighbour buys earplugs.

choices.text: Deny it completely

effects.log: Your spouse looks at you with infinite tenderness and says, 'I know.' You never mention it again.

events.text: Your spouse is away for a week visiting relatives. The house is silent at night. You cannot sleep at all.

choices.text: Admit it when they come home

effects.log: 'I could not sleep without it.' Your spouse snores especially loudly that night, as a kindness.

choices.text: Snore loudly yourself, to keep yourself company

effects.log: It does not work, but it makes you laugh in the dark, which is nearly as good.

events.text: A neighbour's house burned in the winter and they are rebuilding. On the day the ridge beam goes up, the whole lane is supposed to come and haul on the ropes.

choices.text: Haul on the ropes

effects.log: Twenty people on two ropes and a beam as thick as a horse. It goes up on the third pull. Firecrackers, red cloth, and a feast on the half-built floor.

choices.text: Bring the food for the feast

effects.log: You cook for a day for twenty haulers. They eat all of it in the shell of the house, under the new beam, and sing.

events.text: Under the ridge beam, by custom, the builder hides a small red packet of coins and a written wish. The neighbour asks you to write the wish.

choices.text: Write: 'Let no fire find this house'

effects.log: Simple and right. The packet goes up under the beam, and the house stands for a hundred years.

choices.text: Write something funny, to make the house laugh

effects.log: 'May the cat be fat and the in-laws thin.' The neighbour laughs and puts it up anyway. The house is a happy one.

events.text: The house is old now, and being repaired. A young carpenter, taking down the ridge beam, finds the red packet and the wish in your handwriting, and brings it to you.

choices.text: Write a new wish for the new beam

effects.log: Your hand is shaky now. The new wish is shorter and truer: 'Be warm.' The young carpenter puts it up with care.

choices.text: Give the young carpenter the old one to keep

effects.log: The carpenter puts it in a pocket, and you know it will be found again in someone else's beam, years from now.

events.text: Caught in the rain at the ferry landing, you lend your oiled-paper umbrella to a stranger with a baby. You never expect to see it again.

choices.text: Tell them to keep it

effects.log: The stranger bows deeply under the umbrella and goes off into the rain. You walk home soaked and very cheerful.

choices.text: Write your name on the handle first

effects.log: You scratch your name on it with a hairpin. The stranger promises to bring it back. You do not believe it.

events.text: Five years later, a package is left at your gate: your umbrella, mended, oiled, with a little painting of a baby on the paper.

choices.text: Use it, and lend it again

effects.log: You lend it again the next rainy day, to a student. It comes back a year later with a poem on it.

choices.text: Hang it on the wall

effects.log: It hangs by your door, with the baby on it. Visitors ask about it, and you tell the story.

events.text: The umbrella has been lent and returned a dozen times now. It is covered in paintings and poems from everyone who carried it: a baby, a poem, a fish, a mountain. It is famous on the ferry road.

choices.text: Lend it once more, and do not ask for it back

effects.log: It goes off into the rain with a stranger. You hear of it for years after, a long way off, gathering paintings.

choices.text: Paint something on it yourself, finally
